item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers designated outfielder Ryan Ward for assignment ahead of Wednesday’s game, ending his seven-year stay in the Dodgers’ organization.
To replace Ward on the 40-man roster, the Dodgers reinstated trade deadline acquisition Kris Bubic from the 60-day injured list while optioning right-hander Paul Gervase to Triple-A.
Ward, 28, made his MLB debut with the Dodgers this season, but his time in the organization goes well beyond the 20 games he played for the team this season.
He begun making headlines during the 2025 season for his unbelievable performances in Triple-A, with many calling for him to replace outfielder Michael Conforto, who struggled during his one-year tenure in Los Angeles.
Ward won the Pacific Coast League MVP in 2025, hitting 36 homers and driving in 122 runs over the course of 143 games, posting a career-high .937 OPS. He hadn’t appeared in MLB since June prior to his DFA.
Why Did the Dodgers Choose to DFA Ward Over a Pitcher?
While the Dodgers have plenty of pitchers on their 40-man roster, especially some who haven’t performed up to MLB standards this season, so why DFA Ward?
The decision likely comes due to Ward’s positional redundancy. A left-handed outfielder, which the Dodgers have plenty of—especially after calling up Josue De Paula directly from Double-A last week.
The Dodgers view De Paula as the future and already have him in MLB, which effectively put the nail in the coffin for Ward’s time with the Dodgers.
De Paula, the Dodgers’ top prospect, only has five MLB games under his belt, but is turning heads across the league already. He has a homer and three RBIs to go with five walks and a .797 OPS across his five appearances.
How Did Ryan Ward Perform in the Majors?
Ward had a decent year in the majors for the Dodgers, but not quite up to his standards in Triple-A. Through his 20 games, he stepped up to the plate 60 times and posted a .738 OPS.
He hit three homers over the course of those games, driving in 12 runs, though his OPS sat below .300 for all of the final 12 games with the Dodgers.
The 28-year-old got off to a good start with the Dodgers when they called him up for two games in April, logging two hits in his debut and driving in his first MLB RBI.
He came back at the end of May, hitting his first career home run against the Philadelphia Phillies, the. crushed another one against the Los Angeles Angels a few days later. Ward rode a five-game hit streak from June 4-10, but struggled to put up results for the remainder of the year. He logged just four hits over the following 11 games.
Ward returned to the minors at the end of June and had a decent couple of months, but a September slump may have cost him his spot on the 40-man roster. Since Sept. 1, Ward had a .191 batting average with a .565 OPS, hitting just one home run in a hitter-friendly league.
LA can still keep Ward if he clears waivers, but the probability of teams passing on a player with his track record is extremely low.

The Los Angeles Dodgers moved closer to restoring their pitching depth before Wednesday’s series finale against the Cincinnati Reds.
Right-handed starter Roki Sasaki threw a live batting practice session at Great American Ball Park in Cincinnati. Dodgers management is hoping the session clears the last hurdle in Sasaki’s recovery from a right middle-finger blister that has sidelined him since the end of August.
A return to the active roster appears imminent, though the Dodgers haven’t decided whether he’ll resume his rotation spot or shift to the bullpen for the final weeks of the regular season.
Either way, Sasaki is expected to work exclusively out of the bullpen once the playoffs begin.
Sasaki could give manager Dave Roberts’ pitching staff a boost as the Dodgers gear up for October.
Before landing on the injured list, Sasaki posted a 4.60 ERA and 1.33 WHIP with 117 strikeouts over 119.1 innings across 23 starts. He was pulled from his Aug. 26 outing against the Atlanta Braves once the blister appeared. With a fastball averaging 97.8 mph and a plus splitter, Sasaki carries real swing-and-miss upside.
Bullpen an option
Should the Dodgers use him in the bullpen down the stretch, his triple-digit fastball and put-away splitter could bolster L.A.’s late-inning group immediately. Returning him to the rotation alongside Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell would instead add starter depth and help manage workloads over the final two weeks of the regular season.
Keeping Sasaki’s finger healthy is a priority for the Dodgers front office, and avoiding another setback matters as the 24-year-old works his way back. Despite his inconsistent season, Sasaki has shown great stuff and figures to be a key piece of L.A.’s pitching staff as the postseason nears.
A clean live BP outing could lead to a short rehab assignment or a quicker activation before the Dodgers face the San Francisco Giants in their next series. Whether he lands in the rotation or the bullpen for the stretch run, the Dodgers will have another weapon at their disposal heading into October.

item.content:encoded:
山本由伸が「史上最高」の“決定的理由” オーラ溢れる1枚に米国人感動「泣きそう」
今季は敵地での12先発で防御率は1.77と圧倒的
【MLB】ドジャース 4ー0 レッズ（日本時間16日・シンシナティ）
ドジャースの山本由伸投手が15日（日本時間16日）、敵地で行われたレッズ戦に先発登板し、7回1安打無失点の快投で自己最多を更新する14勝目を挙げた。降板直後、MLB公式X（旧ツイッター）が投稿した1枚が米国ファンを虜にした。
初回先頭から2者連続四球を与えたものの無失点で切り抜けると、3回途中から13者連続アウトを奪う圧倒的なピッチングを展開。7回91球を投げ7奪三振無失点で今季21度目のクオリティスタート（QS）を達成した。
降板からわずか8分後、MLB公式Xは今季敵地12先発で防御率「1.77」を誇るデータを公開するとともに、山本の画像を添えた。右腕の凛々しい表情からは“オーラ”すらまとっているように見える。投稿を見た米ファンからは歓喜と絶賛の声が相次いだ。
「我がチームのエースを見て、思わず微笑んだ」
「もうマジで泣きそう」
「奪三振で打ち取りまくって、ファンタジーベースボールのポイントも稼いでくれた」
「史上最高」
「この男、オーラを稼ぎまくってるな」
山本は登板を終え、防御率はリーグ3位の2.51まで改善。サイ・ヤング賞候補の1人としてチームを牽引し、昨年同様にポストシーズンでの活躍に期待される。
（Full-Count編集部）

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Shohei Ohtani, Carlos Correa and more: How star injuries could reshape the MLB playoffs
item.dc:creator: Steve Henson
item.description: - Click here to listen to this article - - As October approaches, injuries and recoveries are poised to reshape the MLB postseason picture, with nearly every contender juggling critical absences and fragile returns. - Houston shuts down Carlos Correa after an ankle setback, the Yankees finally get Max Fried and Aaron Judge back, while Shohei Ohtani looms as the Dodgers’ biggest question. Carlos Correa is out. Max Fried is back. Shohei Ohtani is somewhere in-between. And questions linger ov
item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- As October approaches, injuries and recoveries are poised to reshape the MLB postseason picture, with nearly every contender juggling critical absences and fragile returns.
- Houston shuts down Carlos Correa after an ankle setback, the Yankees finally get Max Fried and Aaron Judge back, while Shohei Ohtani looms as the Dodgers’ biggest question.
Carlos Correa is out. Max Fried is back. Shohei Ohtani is somewhere in-between. And questions linger over the postseason availability of several other MLB difference-makers as October approaches.
Here is a look at the injury status and hopeful returns of impact players on playoff qualifiers and contenders:
American League East
Tampa Bay Rays: Acquired from Baltimore at the trade deadline, swingman Tyler Wells posted a 1.50 earned-run-average before right forearm tightness sidelined him. He is back solely pitching from the bullpen, and could be a key piece for the Rays in their surprising surge to the division title.
Hopeful return: Slick-fielding shortstop Taylor Walls is recovering from a right hip flexor strain and signs point to him returning by October.
The Dodgers clinch a playoff berth with their 4-1 victory over the Cincinnati Reds, reaching the postseason for a record-tying 14th consecutive year.
New York Yankees: The return of staff ace Fried is huge for a team that has clinched a wild-card berth and remains a long step behind the Rays for a division title and first-round bye. The left-hander out of Studio City Harvard-Westlake High gave up one run while walking none over seven innings in his longest start in almost five months. Fried has had two arduous IL stints dealing with a bone bruise on his left elbow.
Hopeful returns: Giancarlo Stanton or Trent Grisham returning in October would give the Yankees lineup additional pop. Three-time AL MVP Aaron Judge has been back for a week since missing more than three months with a fractured rib.
Boston Red Sox: A right quadriceps strain has kept All-Star center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela sidelined for two weeks. However, Rafaela told NESN that he expects to be activated this weekend, a substantial addition to a team that likely will play the Yankees in wild-card series.
Hopeful return: A year ago, Garrett Crochet was 18-5 and led the AL with 205 1/3 innings pitched. This year, left shoulder inflammation and a lat strain have kept him sidelined since April. However, he has ramped up bullpen sessions and is targeting a postseason return as a reliever.
American League Central
Chicago White Sox: The most improved team in baseball is desperately trying to hold off the Guardians and win a division title after finishing last two years in a row. Chicago has enjoyed good health and added journeyman outfielder Tommy Pham from the Phillies on Aug. 31. Pham was activated from the IL on Wednesday and could provide valuable postseason experience to complement his young new teammates — he has hit .315 in 37 career playoff games.
Hopeful return: Drew Thorpe was reinstated from the 60-day IL on Wednesday and is an intriguing option. The right-hander from Cal Poly SLO was a key piece in the 2024 trade that sent Dylan Cease to the Padres but has spent nearly two full seasons on the shelf. Now healthy, his inclusion on the playoff roster would be a gamble that his elite stuff can mask his inexperience.
Cleveland Guardians: Jo Adell didn’t come off the IL, but the addition of the former confounding Angels prospect in an August salary dump has bolstered the Guardians’ outfield — long a problem area. Adell has driven in 28 runs in 38 games with Cleveland and joins glittering rookie Chase DeLauter and steady veteran Steven Kwan in a productive outfield.
Hopeful return: Reliever Shawn Armstrong, who signed a one-year, $5.5 million contract last offseason, has been sidelined since July 24 with a calf strain. Barring a setback in his final minor league rehab appearance, he could be activated in time for the playoffs.
American League West
Houston Astros: Correa, whose second act with Houston has been a flop because of injuries, was working on an accelerated comeback from May ankle surgery. A few days ago team officials expressed optimism, but Tuesday they decided to shelve their shortstop when the ankle became inflamed after a workout. Houston is clinging to a one-game lead over the Texas Rangers in the AL West.
Hopeful return: Nothing of note.
Texas Rangers: Still in contention despite spending much of the season under .500, the Rangers welcomed back pitcher Nathan Eovaldi and third baseman Josh Jung from the injured list over the weekend. A calf strain had kept Jung sidelined since July 21 and Eovaldi had been out since Aug. 7 with elbow inflammation. Eovaldi, who has started in all but 20 of his 339 MLB appearances, will pitch out of the bullpen.
Hopeful return: Nothing of note
National League East
Atlanta Braves: Reynaldo López inflated hopes of a late-career surge when he posted a 1.99 ERA over 25 starts in his first season with Atlanta. But injuries — including right shoulder inflammation this season — have severely limited his contribution. López was placed on the IL again Tuesday.
Hopeful return: Bryce Elder had an arthroscopic procedure to clean up bone fragments in his right knee on Sept. 8. The hope is that the right-handed starter can recover quickly enough to be counted upon in the postseason.
By not putting Shohei Ohtani on the injured list in July or in August, the Dodgers may have compromised the two-way star’s ability to be healthy for the playoffs.
Philadelphia Phillies: Although an MRI found no structural damage to the throwing shoulder of stalwart starter Jesús Luzardo, the left-hander remains a question for the playoffs. He was placed on the 15-day IL retroactive to Sept. 12, and it is doubtful he could pitch again in the regular season. Luzardo has a 2.87 ERA across 29 starts this season.
Hopeful return: Tanner Banks, a major contributor to the Philadelphia bullpen in 2025, was reinstated from the 60-day IL over the weekend. Although he wasn’t effective earlier this season, Banks is welcomed back because Phillies relievers have been poor against left-handed hitters.
National League Central
Milwaukee Brewers: Huntington Beach Marina High product Jake Bauers has suffered from shin splints almost all season, and the pain has kept him from playing the outfield lately. He can play first base, but that takes slugger Andrew Vaughn out of the lineup. Bauers, with 26 home runs and 83 RBIs, has been a key bat for Milwaukee. He has been particularly tough against the Dodgers, batting .348 with a .483 on-base percentage.
Hopeful return: Brandon Woodruff, one of the best starters in baseball when healthy, is rehabbing from shoulder inflammation that sidelined him in July. The Brewers are nearly guaranteed a first-round bye, giving Woodruff an extra week to build stamina.
Chicago Cubs: Shortstop and team leader Dansby Swanson will be welcomed back after missing a month with a left oblique injury. He is expected to rejoin the Cubs during their weekend series against the Cincinnati Reds.
Hopeful return: Left-handed starter Justin Steele is progressing through bullpen sessions and is almost ready to take the mound after missing the entire season with a left elbow flexor strain. Steele, whose record was 16-5 in 2023, likely would pitch from the bullpen in the postseason.
National League West
Dodgers: The loss of center fielder Andy Pages is significant. He can bat near the top or bottom of the order, displays power and speed, and had improved his patience at the plate enough to earn a career-high 45 walks in 128 games.
Hopeful return: Getting Ohtani healthy enough to produce at the plate is a priority, and his absence from the mound shouldn’t be felt if Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal and Tyler Glasnow pitch to their capabilities. Meanwhile, Edwin Diaz might not even make the playoff roster.
Edwin Díaz struggled in his rehab start Sunday, and Dave Roberts is making it clear the Dodgers “got to see something” before putting him on the playoff roster.
San Diego Padres: While recovering from Tommy John surgery, starter Joe Musgrove made it a goal to be ready for the postseason. Recovery difficulties between starts have made his status doubtful, however. Nick Pivetta, on the other hand, has pitched well in two starts since coming off the IL and appears ready.
Hopeful return: Ramón Laurenano, a 2025 trade deadline acquisition with a potent bat, last played May 30 because of hip inflammation. However, he told reporters that the chances of him playing in the postseason are “less than 5%.”
Arizona Diamondbacks: Zac Gallen was activated from the 60-day IL and Michael Soroka from the 15-day IL, giving the D-Backs two starters in their push to win a wild-card berth. Gallen, a proven starter who has been horrendous in 2026, has been out since the All-Star break with elbow inflammation. Soroka was out only two weeks with the same ailment.
Hopeful return: Third baseman Nolan Arenado suffered an injury to his left thumb Tuesday, the same injury he sustained in late August. It’s doubtful the injury would sideline the 14-year veteran with games this week being so important, yet the Diamondbacks have to hope the injury doesn’t impact his productivity.

item.title: [sportingnews.com] Why Tigers likely won't get Tarik Skubal back despite ace's interest in a reunion | Sporting News
item.dc:creator: Matt Sullivan
item.description: Before the 2026 MLB trade deadline, the Detroit Tigers made a massive decision to trade away Tarik Skubal, sending him to the Los Angeles Dodgers in exchange for three prospects. From a long-term perspective, it was the right move. But it still stung. However, Skubal recently mentioned he'd be willing to sign with the Tigers on a long-term deal this offseason. So, maybe the Tigers get the huge return for a Skubal trade and keep him long-term. Tim Kelly of Bleacher Report doesn't think that's goi
item.content:encoded:
Before the 2026 MLB trade deadline, the Detroit Tigers made a massive decision to trade away Tarik Skubal, sending him to the Los Angeles Dodgers in exchange for three prospects. From a long-term perspective, it was the right move. But it still stung.
However, Skubal recently mentioned he'd be willing to sign with the Tigers on a long-term deal this offseason. So, maybe the Tigers get the huge return for a Skubal trade and keep him long-term.
Tim Kelly of Bleacher Report doesn't think that's going to happen, as he points out that the former Tigers Cy Young winner isn't likely to receive a competitive offer from the Tigers this offseason.
Why Tigers not likely to get Tarik Skubal back in free agency despite interest
"Tarik Skubal expressed a willingness to consider the Tigers in free agency," Kelly writes. "... The reality is that Skubal, a Scott Boras client, likely said that knowing that the Tigers won't make him a competitive offer in free agency."
After the Tigers balked at his lofty asking price in arbitration, which resulted in a record-breaking $32 million arbitration hearing, it wouldn't be a surprise if the Tigers balked again on the open market.
Skubal is surely going to be asking for massive, record-breaking money. For a 30-year-old pitcher coming off a mid-season surgery, any record-breaking amount is going to be hard to stomach.
There have been rumors he could land a $400 million deal, and while the Tigers might have interest in Skubal, and he might be interested in a reunion, they're just not likely to make such a massive offer.
Kelly also pointed out how Chris Illitch "hasn't shown the same willingness to spend as his late father did," as a reason why Skubal coming back to Detroit isn't likely.
Signing Skubal to a long-term deal would be a dream scenario for the Tigers, but it's just not likely to happen. Instead, he's more likely to sign with the Dodgers or some other big-market team willing to take the major financial risk with his new deal.
Skubal is going to get a massive payday this offseason, and while the Tigers are a possible landing spot, a reunion doesn't look very likely.
More MLB news:
- Tatsuya Imai predicted not to opt out of $36M Astros contract
- Phillies' Jesus Luzardo on track to be best road pitcher in MLB history since 1913
- Why Braves could trade Spencer Strider this upcoming offseason
- MLB insider accuses Shohei Ohtani of misleading Dodgers about injury issues

The future Hall of Famer had recently missed several games due to injury. That said, Freeman appears to be feeling fine. Reporter: “Freddie, you had those three hits tonight. I know it’s kind of been back and f
item.content:encoded:
On Tuesday night, the Los Angeles Dodgers continued their series with the Cincinnati Reds in Ohio.
The Dodgers won by a score of 4-0.
Freddie Freeman finished with three hits in five at-bats.
Freeman Makes Statement After Game
After the game, Freeman met with the media (via SportsNet LA).
The future Hall of Famer had recently missed several games due to injury.
That said, Freeman appears to be feeling fine.
Reporter: “Freddie, you had those three hits tonight. I know it’s kind of been back and forth for you dealing with this tendinitis, but how is your knee feeling right now, and how good was it to see the results fall today?”
Freeman: “No, it was good. I’ve been kind of working a new thing in the cage the last couple days, so I got to go for results-based things right now. We got to get hot with two weeks to go, and looking to be hot for a few weeks, that’s all I’m trying to do. So I felt good in the cage today, and luckily was able to throw some seeing-eye bleeders out there today.”
Reporter: “With your knee though, are you finding that you still want to give it some time here and there, or is it feeling significantly better?”
Freeman: “I was supposed to be off tomorrow, but I played myself in there. So I’m very excited, I’m in there tomorrow. I think they were trying to manage it. I told them I was good to be able to play every day, but they’re trying to be mindful. I feel good, I had no pain in the knee today. So with three hits today, I got myself in there tomorrow.”
Looking At Freeman Right Now
Freeman was picked in the 2nd round of the 2007 MLB Draft.
He is in the middle of his 5th season with the Dodgers.
Prior to Los Angeles, the ten-time MLB All-Star had a 12-year run with the Atlanta Braves.
Right now, Freeman is batting .296 with 159 hits, 16 home runs, 66 RBIs, 72 runs and seven stolen bases in 143 games.

item.title: [FOX Sports] Teoscar Hernández Is Delivering When The Dodgers Need Him The Most
item.dc:creator: Rowan Kavner
item.description: Teoscar Hernández Is Delivering When The Dodgers Need Him The Most LOS ANGELES — During a months-long spiral at the plate, Teoscar Hernández tried to maintain his upbeat, convivial persona. But for much of the summer, before his September revival, it was difficult for the Dodgers’ fun-loving, seed-tossing veteran presence to look or feel like himself. item.content:encoded:
Teoscar Hernández Is Delivering When The Dodgers Need Him The Most
LOS ANGELES — During a months-long spiral at the plate, Teoscar Hernández tried to maintain his upbeat, convivial persona.
But for much of the summer, before his September revival, it was difficult for the Dodgers’ fun-loving, seed-tossing veteran presence to look or feel like himself.
"I try to stay positive and bring the same energy that you guys know and see everyday — smiling, making jokes," Hernández told me. "But at the same time, it’s really hard."
(Photo by David Jordan/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts noticed his typically jovial outfielder looking a bit more sullen at times, too. It was understandable.
Hernández, a fixture in the Dodgers’ lineup whose clutch hitting, encouraging nature and penchant for performing on the sport’s biggest stage helped his team win back-to-back World Series titles, had a respectable .785 OPS when he went on the injured list on May 29 with a left hamstring strain.
But the 33-year-old did not look the same when he returned a month later. From June 29 to Aug. 29, his .592 OPS was the ninth-lowest mark among all qualified MLB hitters over that stretch.
"Some of the joy was sucked out," Roberts told me, "because it’s hard to be so joyful when you’re not performing. He was still a good teammate, always a good teammate, but I know there were a lot of frustrating moments for him."
Hernández’s struggles were compounded by the fact that the Dodgers were also getting little from their other corner outfielder, Kyle Tucker, or the rest of an offense that looked lifeless for much of the summer.
But now, at a crucial juncture for his team with All-Stars Shohei Ohtani and Andy Pages sidelined, another All-Star in Freddie Freeman battling knee soreness and the playoffs just weeks away, Hernández is taking his frustration out constructively.
He is annihilating the baseball in September, leaving his summer slump behind and giving the Dodgers reason to believe in the depth of their offense again.
"When he catches fire," Dodgers infielder Tommy Edman said, "he’s as good as anybody in the game."
Even among Hernández’s best career stretches, the tear he’s on now stands out. Every part of his offensive profile is enhanced.
Hernández, who’s prone to swing and miss even when he’s going right, is making better swing decisions. From last month to this month, he has lowered his chase rate from 36.7% to 24.8%, tripled his walk rate from 4.3% to 15.1% and cut his strikeout rate nearly in half from 31.2% to 18.9%.
And along with a more selective approach, he is punishing every mistake in a way he couldn’t earlier this season.
Hernández’s hard-hit rate has skyrocketed from 34.5% in July to 47.5% in August to 60% this month. His average exit velocity this September (96.6 mph) is the highest of any month in his career.
Eight of his 10 hardest-hit balls this season have come in the last two weeks, and his power is being generated by the highest average bat speed he has produced in any month over the last two seasons (74.1 mph).
It’s a far cry from where Hernández was just a couple of weeks ago, when his year-long struggle against right-handers had the Dodgers considering using a platoon in left field. That no longer appears to be a consideration.
"Right now," Roberts said, "it’s just night and day."
So how, exactly, did Hernández find his way back?
"The most important part, he’s healthy," Dodgers infielder Miguel Rojas told me. "If he’s healthy, we can see the Teo that’s running hard on the bases, stealing bases, going first to third. Obviously the bat is there because it’s his best tool, but seeing the complete player now is really refreshing."
Earlier this season, Hernández’s downturn looked familiar.
A year ago, he had the highest batting average on the team when he went on the IL in May with an adductor strain. He returned two weeks later, then watched his OPS precipitously drop 200 points from May 21 (.927) to July 21 (.727).
Clearly, the lower-body injury had lingered, throwing off his swing and sapping his power.
This year, it was happening again, only with his hamstring. The swing that worked for him before the injury was putting too much pressure on his lower half. Upon his return from the IL, he had a .562 OPS overall in July and a team-worst .496 OPS against right-handed pitching in August.
"I told Dave, ‘If you feel like you have to use somebody else in there, just do it,’" Hernández said.
(Photo by Meg Oliphant/Getty Images)
That would not be necessary. At least, not again after Aug. 25. The decision to sit him that day was noteworthy, considering the Dodgers were coming off an off day and facing a Braves team they were battling for a first-round bye.
In hindsight, it might have served as a wake-up call.
On Aug. 26, Hernández returned to the lineup in Atlanta with a two-hit day. He then ended the Dodgers’ next series in Detroit with a two-run homer off Framber Valdez, which might have been the turning point.
"I think that at-bat gave him the extra life that he needed for the last part of the season," Rojas said. "Obviously, baseball is about confidence, and you find confidence with success, and I thought that’s what he needed. He needed, like, one good swing that he knows he’s back, and then all of a sudden we see the results we get now."
There’s also a mechanical component to Hernández’s upswing.
Too often, Hernández felt both rushed and late at the plate as he worked his way back from his hamstring injury. He has since opened his stance in an effort, he says, to slow his body up, prevent his front hip from flying open and give him more time to see the ball. He has also traded his more subtle toe tap for a slightly more exaggerated leg lift and hip twist as a timing mechanism that seems to be producing more power.
These were moves he used before in his career. Now healthy, he feels his body can withstand the added force once again.
Sometimes with hitting, the littlest tweaks can yield the biggest results.
"That’s why it’s hard," Hernández told me. "One day, you don’t know what you’re doing. The next day, you change barely — sometimes it’s your hands, sometimes it’s your legs, sometimes it’s how low, how tall [in the stance] — and it can click, and you go on a heater."
Even compared to heaters of the past, though, this one is unlike most for Hernández. If September ended today, his 1.211 OPS this month would be the highest mark in any month of his career.
Hernández maintains that his confidence never wavered through the rough patch; that he knew, at some point, things would turn. His teammates shared that belief.
This was the same guy, after all, who homered in every playoff series last season.
(Photo by Melina Pizano/Getty Images)
"The clutch gene and everything that he has in him, the reason why we got him and the reason why we’ve been so good with him in the lineup the last couple years, nothing changed this year just because of a bad stretch," Rojas told me. "To be honest with you, I was never concerned about it … I want nobody in a big at-bat more than Teo."
After the big hit last month in Detroit, Hernández returned home, made the swing changes and provided the elusive clutch hit the scuffling Dodgers’ offense had been missing with a walk-off double to salvage a series against the Cardinals.
That hit helped spark an eight-game winning streak for the Dodgers, who started to look like themselves again.
Their ebullient left fielder is looking that way, too.
"I feel really good right now," Hernández said. "I’ve been working really hard for this, and I’m glad and happy that everything is coming together."

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are looking to win their series against the Cincinnati Reds on Wednesday.
The Dodgers took Monday's series opener, 4-1, behind seven shutout innings from Tarik Skubal. Then, they won Tuesday's game, 4-0, behind seven shutout innings from Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
On Wednesday, LA has another superstar pitcher on the mound in left-hander Blake Snell.
“When you’re writing in the lineup and you see those guys, and one trying to up the other guy, and then now you got Snell going [Wednesday] — you feel good about preventing runs,” manager Dave Roberts said.
“A team like the Reds right now, where they’re scuffling a little bit, it’s daunting when you see a starter like those guys that we’re running out there.”
Dodgers vs Reds Pitching Matchup on Wednesday
Snell is looking to continue his run of dominance since returning from midseason elbow surgery.
The left-hander has gone 4-0 with a 1.04 ERA across six starts, striking out 46 while allowing zero home runs over 34.2 innings of work.
Snell, who pitched 5.2 innings in his most recent start, is still looking to go deeper into games moving forward. He hasn't pitched more than six innings in any of his six starts.
“I mean the goal, at worst is definitely six for me,” Snell said. “I also know that I can go seven, eight, nine. I know I’m able to do it. So for me not to, I just have to get more efficient early in the game. I feel like once I get past the first couple innings, I start cruising and start figuring it out."
Opposite Snell will be left-hander Andrew Abbott, who's 6-11 with a 4.78 ERA and 120 strikeouts over 154.1 innings this season.
He's allowed seven earned runs in two of his last three starts, and has a 7.71 ERA since the start of August.
Dodgers Starting Lineup
- Tommy Edman, CF
- Mookie Betts, SS
- Will Smith, C
- Freddie Freeman, 1B
- Teoscar Hernández, DH
- Miguel Rojas, 2B
- Kyle Tucker, RF
- Kiké Hernández, 3B
- Alex Call, LF
Josue De Paula, Max Muncy and Alex Freeland are out of the lineup with the left-handed pitcher on the mound.
How to Watch Dodgers vs Reds on Wednesday
First pitch for Los Angeles Dodgers vs. Cincinnati Reds on Wednesday, Sept. 16 is 3:40 p.m. PT/6:40 p.m. ET.
The game will be broadcast on SportsNet LA and in the MLB app.
The game will be broadcast on the radio on AM570 (in English) and KTNQ 1020 AM (in Spanish).
Sign up for our free newsletter and follow us on X/Twitter and Facebook for the latest news.
Noah Camras graduated from the University of Southern California in 2022 with a B.A. in Journalism and a minor in sports media studies. He was born and raised in Los Angeles and has extensively covered Southern California sports in his career. Noah is the publisher of Dodgers on SI after contributing as a writer and editor over the last three years.

item.content:encoded:
gambit – noun
a chess opening in which a player risks one or more pawns or a minor piece to gain an advantage in position
Now, if your mind immediately went to the Marvel Comics character and you were confused, fair enough. Here's the clip you likely thought of, so we can all feel better and get to the heart of the essay.
And for the record, Freddie Freeman is hardly a minor piece, but giving up a major piece for tactical advantage is called a sacrifice, which wouldn't be appropriate given the circumstances here, as Freeman returned to the lineup for the September 15 game against the Cincinnati Reds.
A funny thought occurred to me while watching Freddie Freeman these last few months:
"Where did his power go? He sure seems like he's hitting into more double plays than I remember."
Looking at Freeman's stats for the year, apart from the power and RBI numbers being down a bit, nothing looks amiss. Honestly, I originally dismissed the feeling that something was wrong because Freeman was hitting up a storm for about a month after the All-Star Break.
There wasn't much power behind it, but when someone has a slash line of .367/.402/.411 over 24 games starting from the All-Star Break, pointing out fault feels like searching for a fly in the ointment. Yes, Freeman only had four doubles, eight RBIs, and nearly three times as many strikeouts as walks, but the overall body of work looked pretty good.
Freeman had a solid couple of games in Denver where he hit for doubles power and used the entire field. However, since the Denver series, where Freeman was hitting for average, he's just not.
When you aren't hitting for either average or power, alarm bells tend to finally ring.
Power drained
On September 9, Freeman was kept out of the lineup for right knee soreness and was considered day-to-day. To his credit, Dave Roberts did mention Freeman's slump on September 9.
Roberts said there was no one incident that caused Freeman's knee soreness, but he believes it has impacted his performance at the plate lately.
"Freddie does a really good job of hitting against his front side, and then when you can't do that with your front side, your right knee, then you're compromised," Roberts said. "I see there's a lot more swing-and-miss the last few days. That's just not who he is."
In the 18 games since the Colorado series until the start of play on September 15, Freeman has a slash line of .215/.338/.292. He does have his only home run of the second half, and his strikeouts-to-walk ratio is about 1.5/1 instead of 3/1 earlier in the year.
The problem is more of the eye test: Freeman is starting to finally look, and maybe move, like his age.
The splits on Baseball Savant from last year to now tell a pretty glaring tale: if you want to beat Freeman in 2026, go low and in. Also, Freeman feasted on center-cut pitches last year, not so this year.
I'm not a hitting expert, but having a diminished knee would make it harder to rotate to hit stuff middle in. On the September 13 broadcast of the finale against the Miami Marlins, Dontrelle Willis pointed out how Freeman is compromised rotationally generally, as pitches he would normally drive the other way are being weakly hit.
Even after Freeman hit a career-high and now league-high in double plays on Sunday, the Dodgers are not seriously entertaining putting Freeman on the injured list, per Katie Woo of The Athletic:
"I think it's one of those things where we've got to manage it … just pick spots to give him an off day here or there," Roberts said. "Again, we've just got to make sure he's at optimal health when we finish the season. So I think that he might not love it, but giving him a day off here or there might be beneficial."
The Dodgers don't believe an IL stint is necessary. Instead, Roberts is working in frequent off days. That's rare for Freeman, who hasn't played in fewer than 147 games in any season as a Dodger. Freeman had a scheduled day off over the Dodgers' previous nine-game homestand and also served as the designated hitter twice in that span. He wasn't in the lineup in the last game of the homestand on Wednesday, and following a team travel day, he also sat out Friday's game.
[Emphasis added.]
Freeman insists he feels fine.
Freeman hitting into two double plays and having a key miscue that contributed to the season and series loss to the Miami Marlins seems to indicate otherwise. It's worth noting that Freeman hit another tailor-made ground ball to second on a pitcher's pitch in his final at-bat that likely would have turned into another double play had Mookie Betts not doubled earlier in the frame.
"Just talking to him today, he said he felt good," Roberts said. "Obviously, the swings don't indicate that, don't validate that. On the defense, he's obviously not moving as well as he's used to.
"I think that he's doing anything and everything he can to prepare. But yeah, the last week, it's pretty obvious that he's not himself in the box."
Freeman won't be in Monday's starting lineup, Roberts said, but should play Tuesday…
[Emphasis added.]
Much like the sense one had when watching the Americanized remake of the original 1954 classic Gojira, Godzilla: King of the Monsters, one would expect a sense of deja vu right now, even with character actor Raymond Burr long dead.
Japanese Original, American Remake
I am typically not one to mince words, and I shall not do so here. Along with Dustin Nosler of Dodgers Digest, I was dead on the money regarding the Dodgers' malpractice in not acting decisively on Ohtani and his reluctance to admit injury in the face of personal dogma of success.
I argued that the Dodgers had bungled spectacularly, and events worked themselves out to prove my initial hypothesis correct on all fronts. Now the team has backed itself into a corner regarding Ohtani.
Contrary to what some might think, I did not enjoy being right. Frankly, I am correct often enough that I do not need the constant validation, unless it comes from either the Dodgers broadcast team or national media. (In which case, gimme.)
On September 11, Katie Woo of The Athletic wrote an op-ed recently that pulled few punches:
Nobody is blameless in the Shohei Ohtani injury saga. Not the Los Angeles Dodgers' front office, which should have been more proactive in protecting the team's biggest star. Not Ohtani, who downplayed the severity of his symptoms. And while hindsight is always 20-20, there were warning signs throughout the last few weeks that suggested a stint on the injured list was the safest course of action if the organization wanted to give its prized star the best possible chance at healing in time to begin the Dodgers' quest to win three straight World Series.
As the Dodgers prepare to be without Ohtani until Sept. 23 at the earliest, their biggest concern has become a reality. When Ohtani — who is expected to be placed on the injured list on Friday — does return, there is no guarantee he'll be in optimal condition for the postseason.
[Emphasis added.]
Um, excuse me? To quote one of the finest bits of media from the 2010s, I get to channel Chris Taylor for once and declare the following:
I know, Ms. Woo means nobody relevant, but words matter, and any excuse for referential comedy is a good one.
"I think that if it were a postseason game tomorrow, (Ohtani) would be in the lineup," manager Dave Roberts said Wednesday afternoon, hours before announcing Ohtani would be placed on the IL. "I think that now you're talking about two weeks, 14 days. I feel that that's substantial. He'll be in a much better place than he was today. Is it going to be to 100 percent? Probably not. But I do think that with this time that we're taking now he'll be in an adequate spot to finish the season."
Adequate is a far cry from healthy. It is fair to question how Ohtani was handled in the second half. Should he have attempted a pitching comeback, knowing his physical health was limited? Should the Dodgers have stopped that push sooner, or placed him on the injured list earlier? In their first season of managing Ohtani as a full-season two-way player, there was always going to be some trial and error. That was acknowledged from the start of the season by both Roberts and president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman. And in fairness, there was a cognizant effort to keep Ohtani as rested as possible, including a season-long six-man rotation and an attempt to maneuver Ohtani's starts to line up on games prior to a team off day, when possible.
Hindsight is generally 20/20. I am sure if the Dodgers were armed with foreknowledge in a do-over, they would not have Ohtani's best pitching starts of the year be in Houston and San Francisco … in May.
At the risk of retreading previously covered ground, we shall conclude this portion with Roberts' regret, especially considering that Ohtani tweaked his arm in his last played game and did not immediately tell anyone about it:
Looking back, it is something Roberts wish happened a week ago.
"I think if we look right now, here today, I would love to go back and put him on the IL," the manager said. "But I did feel at that moment in time, we all felt that giving him four days was sufficient. He was agreeable. Getting him out there on Monday with the hope that he would be able to play tonight. But where we're at right now, sure."
The Dodgers should have followed their own advice or learned from their handling of Ohtani to send Freeman back to Los Angeles for ten days before arriving in Cincinnati.
They didn't.
The Dodgers have calculated that whatever value Freeman can generate in the waning days of the season is greater than the potential benefit of having Freeman recuperate for ten days, having three days against the already-eliminated San Francisco Giants to use as a tune-up. Hence, the title of this essay: the Freeman Gambit.
Yesterday's game showed promise, even with a couple of moments that made one grimace. Freeman talked about how his three-hit performance likely ensured he would play on September 16.
Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic reported Roberts' comments on the health issues of players like Ohtani, Freeman, and Edgardo Henriquez after the Dodgers clinched their fourteenth consecutive postseason appearance:
"I think right now it's front of mind, it's not great," Roberts said. "But I will say this: Once you get to October, athletes have a magical way of feeling better. It happens every single year, where there's that extra adrenaline that athletes get when you get to the postseason."
The Dodgers still boast what is likely baseball's most talented roster and an established track record of postseason success that might be enough to make history. That was the heart of Roberts' toast: that the Dodgers have not yet played their best baseball.
They still can.
"We just haven't really gotten everyone all synced up at the same time," Muncy said. "So it is a scary thought to think what we could possibly do if we did that. So hopefully that's still ahead for us at the right time."
Whether the Freeman Gambit pays off over the next two weeks before the upcoming postseason tournament is an open question. Gambits are risky, even when they work.

item.content:encoded:
This article is a part of Verducci’s View, a new weekly baseball newsletter from Sports Illustrated senior writer Tom Verducci. Every Monday, Tom empties out his notebook over email and covers MLB’s hottest topics, provides in-depth analysis through both text and video breakdowns, looks forward to what’s worth watching during the week and more. If you want to be featured in his new mailbag, please email newsletters@si.com with any questions about MLB or his decades in the sport.
📺 Breakdown of the Week
One of the many fascinating revelations Tarik Skubal shared with me for our upcoming SI cover piece was how he puts his entire trust in his catcher when it comes to pitch selection. That approach becomes more interesting when you change teams midseason. Skubal had more catchers in his first seven starts with the Dodgers (Hunter Feduccia, Ben Rortvedt and Will Smith) than he did in his previous 70 starts with the Tigers (Dillon Dingler and Jake Rogers).
A pattern has emerged in how the Dodgers’ catchers call pitches for Skubal as compared to the Tigers’ choices: he is leaning more into his changeup (his best pitch) and backing off his sinker (his fourth best pitch). He threw more changeups in his first month with Los Angeles (179) than he did in any month in his career. As the following chart shows, his use of his changeup has risen from 25.1% to 28.8%.
Skubal’s tweak to his arsenal as a Dodger is even more interesting when you dive into what he throws when he’s in trouble. With the Tigers, Skubal threw his four-seamer more than any other pitch with runners in scoring position (37%). With the Dodgers, the changeup has been his No. 1 choice with RISP (36%).
Skubal Pitch Choice with RISP, 2026
| Pitch Type | Tigers | Dodgers | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Four-seam fastball | 37% | 33% | -4% |
| Changeup | 29% | 36% | +7% |
| Slider | 14% | 14% | - |
| Sinker | 20% | 14% | -6% |
| Curveball | 1% | 3% | +2% |
Like the Rays, the Dodgers believe in leaning into your best pitch, especially in tight spots. How good is Skubal’s changeup? It has the highest whiff rate of any changeup in MLB (46.8%). It also is among the very best at getting out of jams:
Lowest Avg Allowed on Changeups with RISP, 2026 (Min. 125 pitches)
| Pitcher | No. of Changeups | BA |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Bradgley Rodriguez, Padres | 162 | .108 |
| 2. Tarik Skubal, Doders | 121 | .128 |
| 3. Martin Perez, Braves | 186 | .132 |
| 4. Eduardo Rodriguez, D-Backs | 174 | .133 |
📺 TV on TV This Week
Thursday, Sept. 17: Phillies at Mets, 7:15 p.m. ET (Fox)
Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor arrived in the big leagues in 2015 as a premier defender with questions about how much pop he had in his bat. Across 416 minor league games he hit just 23 home runs and slugged .387.
Eleven years later, Lindor is one of the greatest power hitting shortstops in the history of the game who is on the Hall of Fame highway. His career slugging in the majors is .472, behind only Joe Cronin (.475) among shortstops with at least 1,500 games at the position.
His next home run will be career No. 300. He will become only the 27th player with 300 home runs and 200 stolen bases, but the first with 1,500 games at shortstop.
Lindor has hit 292 of his home runs while playing shortstop, tying him with Miguel Tejada for third on the all-time list and within range of passing Alex Rodriguez (344) and Cal Ripken Jr. (346) to become the all-time home run leader while playing shortstop.
Tom Verducci is a senior writer for Sports Illustrated who has covered Major League Baseball since 1981. He also serves as an analyst for FOX Sports and the MLB Network; is a New York Times best-selling author; and cohosts The Book of Joe podcast with Joe Maddon. A five-time Emmy Award winner across three categories (studio analyst, reporter, short form writing) and nominated in a fourth (game analyst), he is a three-time National Sportswriter of the Year winner, two-time National Magazine Award finalist, and a Penn State Distinguished Alumnus Award recipient. Verducci is a member of the National Sports Media Hall of Fame, Baseball Writers Association of America (including past New York chapter chairman) and a Baseball Hall of Fame voter since 1993. He also is the only writer to be a game analyst for World Series telecasts. He lives in New Jersey with his wife, with whom he has two children.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers have glaring problems as playoffs approach — but also the threefold remedy
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez
item.description: The Dodgers will be in every game they play in October, and that alone means they will enter the playoffs as the favorites to win the World Series. Not because of Shohei Ohtani. Not because of Freddie Freeman. And certainly not because of their bullpen. There were a number of alarming developments in the last week or so, but if any team is designed to survive them, it’s the Dodgers. Whatever their problems, they still have the best rotation in baseball. No player influences the outcome of a game
item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers will be in every game they play in October, and that alone means they will enter the playoffs as the favorites to win the World Series.
Not because of Shohei Ohtani. Not because of Freddie Freeman. And certainly not because of their bullpen.
There were a number of alarming developments in the last week or so, but if any team is designed to survive them, it’s the Dodgers.
Whatever their problems, they still have the best rotation in baseball.
No player influences the outcome of a game as much as a starting pitcher, and the Dodgers are the only team that will be able to roll out one Cy Young Award-caliber arm after another after another.
The Dodgers were negligent with Ohtani, and the verdict on their management of Freeman is pending, but they at least set up their pitchers the right way.
The rotation is more than a collection of big names. In Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell, the Dodgers have three starters who are peaking in time to deliver the kinds of performances that will be required for them to win their third consecutive World Series.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto pitched seven shutout innings on Tuesday in a 4-0 win over the Cincinnati Reds, marking his third consecutive seven-inning start.
“I feel really good and I don’t have any physical problems,” Yamamoto told reporters in Japanese. “I want to treat practice each and every day with importance and go into October in the best condition.”
Yamamoto isn’t alone.
The day before Yamamoto’s start, Tarik Skubal pitched seven scoreless innings of his own in a 4-1 victory over the Reds. In his previous start, which was also against the Reds but at Dodger Stadium, Skubal pitched 7 ⅓ innings.
“Just getting in a rhythm,” Skubal said.
Blake Snell, who is scheduled to take his turn in the rotation on Wednesday, was 4-0 with a 1.04 earned-run average in the six games he started since returning from an elbow cleanup that cost him three months.
The one source of concern in the rotation is Tyler Glasnow, who, like Snell, was slow-played in his return from an injury. Sidelined for 3 ½ months because of back problems, Glasnow showed promise in his first couple of starts after he came back. But in his last two starts, he gave up a combined eight runs, 11 hits and seven walks in 10 innings. But as the team’s No. 4 starter, he is unlikely to start more than one game in any postseason series.
Even before Ohtani was placed on the injured list because of right arm and left knee injuries, the starting pitching was likely going to have to carry the Dodgers – much as it did last year.
Recent developments have shifted even more of the burden to the starting pitchers.
Edwin Diaz, their $69-million closer, was blow-torched for five runs in ⅔ of an inning in the most recent game of his minor-league rehabilitation assignment. At this point, he’s a longshot to make the postseason roster.
Diaz’s failure to rediscover his All-Star form will have major ramifications on the bullpen, which lost ninth-inning candidate Edgardo Henriquez to a lower-back problem for the remainder of the regular season. Henriquez’s status for the playoffs remains a mystery.
Manager Dave Roberts’ current ninth-inning choice, Tanner Scott, is in a minor slump, as he has given up runs in five of his last 12 apperances.
While the Dodgers will have to find a closer – Roki Sasaki? – their ability to create favorable matchups in the innings before the ninth is also under question. The simplest way to address those uncertainties will be for the starters to pitch deeper into games. Last year, Yamamoto pitched a complete game in the National League Championship Series and another in his next start in the World Series. Snell had an eight-inning start in the NLCS.
The greater problem could be the already-inconsistent offense, which could go into the playoffs with physically-compromised versions of Ohtani and Freeman.
Freeman missed three of five games before starting at first base on Tuesday. Freeman collected three hits in the game, but he’s 37 years old and the Dodgers can’t be certain how his right knee will hold up.
As for Ohtani, Roberts reported on Tuesday that he resumed baseball activities. Roberts said he expected Ohtani to return before the end of the regular season, but hedged his prediction.
“Whether it happens or not,” Roberts said, “is to be determined.”
If the Dodgers don’t know if Ohtani will be able to even step into the batter’s box next week, how could they possibly count on him to be a consistent source of offense?
They can’t.
In other words, the margin for error could be miniscule for the Dodgers. Their starting pitchers might have to be close to perfect. The challenge will be formidable. But considering who will be pitching for them, it will be very much in the realm of possibility.

item.content:encoded:
Shohei Ohtani sigue dando buenos pasos en su rehabilitación al realizar práctica de bateo desde este martes en Los Ángeles. El mánager de los Dodgers, Dave Roberts, confirmó que la estrella nipona evoluciona favorablemente y se mantiene firme en su objetivo de volver a la acción antes del cierre de la temporada regular.
Sobre el doble agente del conjunto, expresó: «Shohei realizó sus swings en el tee y la respuesta física fue muy positiva (…) No tenemos una fecha exacta para su reaparición en el lineup, pero avanzamos con un progreso constante día a día. Lo importante es que el entrenamiento de hoy representó un avance claro», dijo.
El oriundo de Oshu, permanece en la lista de lesionados desde el pasado 8 de septiembre debido a una molestia muscular en el bíceps derecho y fue descartado para volver a lanzar durante la temporada debido a una lesión en su rodilla. La sesión de este martes marcó su primer trabajo con el bate desde que fue apartado de la plantilla activa.
Lee también: Yoshinobu Yamamoto sacó su poder en la lomita
Aunque el nipón no acompañó al conjunto angelino en su gira como visitante por Cincinnati, continúa completando su plan de trabajo y terapia médica en las instalaciones del conjunto de California.
Con el boleto a los playoffs ya asegurado para Los Ángeles, el cuerpo técnico confía en contar con Ohtani para los compromisos finales del calendario regular y ponerlo a punto de cara a la lucha por el título.

item.title: [dodgerblue.com] Injured list stint for Freddie Freeman doesn't 'make sense at all'
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Abdón Ibarra
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers have allowed Freddie Freeman to play through a right knee injury as of late, while occasionally taking him out of the lineup when they see fit. The Dodgers took a similar approach with Shohei Ohtani’s various ailments, but the team has been slightly more willing to rest Freeman compared to the four-time MVP. Given the way Ohtani’s health regressed while continuing to play through injury, it begs the question of whether the Dodgers are making the same mistake with Freeman.
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have allowed Freddie Freeman to play through a right knee injury as of late, while occasionally taking him out of the lineup when they see fit.
The Dodgers took a similar approach with Shohei Ohtani’s various ailments, but the team has been slightly more willing to rest Freeman compared to the four-time MVP.
Given the way Ohtani’s health regressed while continuing to play through injury, it begs the question of whether the Dodgers are making the same mistake with Freeman.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts acknowledged the concern over the weekend, but believes Freeman’s situation is different and does not necessitate a trip to the injured list.
“I think that’s certainly a valid question,” Roberts said on SportsNet LA. “I just think that right now with where we’re at in the season, an IL is not an option in the sense of I personally don’t think we have a better option. So I don’t think it needs to be 10 days, but could it be more than one?
“That’s a fair question. I’ve got to talk to the training staff, Freddie, and ultimately make that decision. But I don’t think an IL makes sense at all.”
Both Roberts and Freeman previously confirmed the knee injury is affecting the 37-year-old at the plate and in the field. The good news is that resting Freeman for just a couple of days has proven to reduce the severity of discomfort.
The Dodgers are not concerned with the injury getting worse, but they will continue to monitor his condition to make sure that remains the case. Before Tuesday’s game, Roberts said he would be watching each of Freeman’s at-bats closely to evaluate his right knee.
Freeman said his knee felt better heading into Tuesday’s contest after missing Monday’s game.
“Feels better today than he did yesterday, which is a good thing. I’ll re-evaluate after tonight,” Roberts began. “But obviously, there’s a day game on Thursday, so just kind of being mindful because I want him in that game on Thursday. I’ll be watching him closely.”
Dodgers need Freddie Freeman down the stretch
The Dodgers still have plenty to play for this season after clinching their 14th consecutive playoff berth.
L.A. is also closing in on another National League West title, but they still have work to do to clinch a top-two seed in the National League. Securing a first-round bye would be significant for the Dodgers, given the current injuries to Ohtani, Freeman and others.
If you love our reporting, choose DodgerBlue.com as a preferred source on Google.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers’ Kyle Tucker Signing Summed Up In 1 Painful Word
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: Everyone knew the Los Angeles Dodgers paid more to sign Kyle Tucker than anyone else in MLB was willing to pay. Even still, it seemed like the deal would be a good one for the back-to-back World Series champs. Tucker has been a multi-tool outfielder for his entire career, and now he'd be joined a stacked lineup that would, if anything, take some pressure off of him. It sure seemed like a no-brainer for everyone involved. Somehow, though, it has been a disaster. The Dodgers are still great, of co
item.content:encoded:
Everyone knew the Los Angeles Dodgers paid more to sign Kyle Tucker than anyone else in MLB was willing to pay.
Even still, it seemed like the deal would be a good one for the back-to-back World Series champs. Tucker has been a multi-tool outfielder for his entire career, and now he'd be joined a stacked lineup that would, if anything, take some pressure off of him.
It sure seemed like a no-brainer for everyone involved.
Somehow, though, it has been a disaster. The Dodgers are still great, of course, but Tucker hasn't contributed to that.
And so in an article earlier this week, ESPN's Bradford Doolittle summarized the disappointing signings of Tucker and closer Edwin Diaz in a single word:
"Ouch."
Yeah, that about sums it up.
Kyle Tucker Stats
Through Sept. 15, Tucker has played 143 games for the Dodgers. You've got to give him credit for showing up every day and trying to break out of a funk that seems never-ending.
For the season, he has batted just .226, though.
Tucker has slugged OK, at least, with 21 doubles, four triples and 15 home runs to give him a .701 OPS.
He also has stolen 11 bases without getting caught.
The problem is that Tucker signed a deal worth $60 million per year, and he's on pace for by far the lowest OPS of his career outside of a 28-game debut stint in 2018.
"The Dodgers' splash signings of Tucker and Edwin Diaz in last season's free agency were the cause of much handwringing about L.A.'s economic dominance," Doolittle writes. "While those high-level, targeted acquisitions looked like no-brainers at the time, the first year of both deals could hardly have gone worse. Together, Tucker and Diaz are at minus-1.0 bWAR for their Dodgers debuts while earning a combined $47 million. Ouch."
Tucker has homered twice in the last five games for the Dodgers, dating back to Sept. 11, so maybe it's a sign that he's heating up at just the right time.
It sure would be ironic if Tucker just coasted through a disappointing season but then stepped up in time to help them win the World Series again.
Edwin Diaz Stats
Diaz has dealt with injuries most of the season and is currently on the 15-day IL, but even when conceptually healthy, he's been rough.
In 16 outings, Diaz has an 11.86 ERA. He's allowed 18 runs (including three homers) in 13.1 innings. Diaz has also walked 10 guys, and while he's struck out 19, the punchouts haven't been enough to overcome the other issues.
At this point, it's not clear whether Diaz can be any kind of help down the stretch and into October.
The Dodgers rolled last postseason with a bullpen that relied on starting pitchers for the most part, and that may have to be the case again.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Kyle Tucker, Edwin Diaz Earn Title Nobody Wants for Dodgers
item.dc:creator: Ricardo Sandoval; Unknown
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers had yet another dream offseason in 2025-26. The Dodgers were once again viewed as the winners of the offseason, earning the honor among media and fans for the third straight year after signing closer Edwin Diaz and star outfielder Kyle Tucker. Diaz and Tucker signed lucrative contracts with the Dodgers; however, neither has panned out anywhere close to where the Dodgers had hoped. Instead, ESPN's Bradford Doolittle labeled the two as the biggest disappointment for the Dod
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers had yet another dream offseason in 2025-26.
The Dodgers were once again viewed as the winners of the offseason, earning the honor among media and fans for the third straight year after signing closer Edwin Diaz and star outfielder Kyle Tucker.
Diaz and Tucker signed lucrative contracts with the Dodgers; however, neither has panned out anywhere close to where the Dodgers had hoped.
Instead, ESPN's Bradford Doolittle labeled the two as the biggest disappointment for the Dodgers as the regular season winds down.
"The Dodgers' splash signings of Tucker and Edwin Diaz in last season's free agency were the cause of much handwringing about LA's economic dominance," Doolittle wrote.
"While those high-level, targeted acquisitions looked like no-brainers at the time, the first year of both deals could hardly have gone worse. Together, Tucker and Diaz are at minus-1.0 bWAR for their Dodgers debuts while earning a combined $47 million. Ouch."
How Has Edwin Diaz Been for the Dodgers?
Diaz was the first of the two to sign, inking a three-year, $69 million contract with the Dodgers.
The Dodgers made him the highest-paid closer by average annual salary, and as the season winds down, that contract is looking like an utter disaster. In 16 appearances this year, Diaz has posted a 11.85 ERA, 2.56 WHIP and 19 strikeouts in 13.2 innings.
The 32-year-old has blown four saves out of 11 opportunities. On top of that, batters are hitting a staggering .385 against him in Los Angeles.
Diaz has also struggled with injuries. He's missed significant time due to elbow surgery and is currently on the injured list with neck inflammation.
His lack of results, inconsistencies and injuries have cast serious doubt on whether he will even make the Dodgers' postseason roster.
How Has Kyle Tucker Been for the Dodgers?
As for Tucker, he's been available, but just hasn't performed.
The Dodgers signed the 29-year-old to a lucrative deal, carrying the highest present-day average annual value (AAV) in MLB history at $57.1 million per year.
However, Tucker hasn't performed at that level for most of the season.
The overall numbers alone are worrisome. Tucker is batting .226 with 15 home runs, 66 RBIs, 11 stolen bases and 113 hits in 500 at-bats. His OPS is just .701.
Tucker will continue to get everyday opportunities through the end of the regular season and the posteason. If he can play well in October, all will be forgotten from his disappointing first year.

Ricardo Sandoval is a freelance writer with On SI. He is a graduate of California State University, Northridge, and specializes in sports writing, particularly in MLB, NBA and NFL. He previously served as an Associate Editor for Dodgers Nation and has worked with Newsweek and The Sporting News.

And it doesn’t get much easier with Blake Snell taking the mound, as the Dodgers are one win away from sweeping the Reds in a fourth straight series dating back to last year—counting both the regular season and playoffs. Considering Sunday’s loss to the Marlins in which Emmet Sheehan pitched quite well, Dodger starters have held oppon
item.content:encoded:
The colloquially called “Great American Small Park” has looked awfully big for the Cincinnati Reds hitters facing the best pitching that the Dodgers have to offer. And it doesn’t get much easier with Blake Snell taking the mound, as the Dodgers are one win away from sweeping the Reds in a fourth straight series dating back to last year—counting both the regular season and playoffs.
Considering Sunday’s loss to the Marlins in which Emmet Sheehan pitched quite well, Dodger starters have held opponents scoreless through 20 innings, 14 of which have come against starters Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto. On top of being dominant, Skubal and Yamamoto share the fact that they deviated somewhat from their regular approach in their last outing against the Reds, but in opposite directions—Skubal leaning more heavily on the fastball, while Yamamoto threw it even less than he normally does.
A critical distinction must be made between these two previous starters and Snell. Unlike the pair, Snell will be facing the Reds for the first time this season since he was not on the schedule in the three-game series at Dodger Stadium last week. And speaking of a track record against the Reds, Snell will have fond memories of his last time pitching at this stadium. Back in 2024, still with the Giants, Snell delivered one of the greatest outings of his career when he shut out the Reds in a 3-0 win—the two-time Cy Young winner punched out 11 in what, to this day, remains the only complete game and the only shutout of Snell’s illustrious career.
Wednesday game info
- Teams: Dodgers at Reds
- Ballpark: Great American Ball Park, Cincinnati
- Start time: 3:40 p.m. PT
- TV: SportsNet LA
- Radio: AM 570 (English), KTNQ 1020 AM (Spanish)

Most recently, they won by a score of 4-0 on Tuesday.
Bob Nightengale of USA Today wrote: “The Los Angeles Dodgers can clinch their 13th division title in 14 years with a victory over Cincinnati today or a loss later at night by the San Diego Padres
Los Angeles Dodgers Announced Andy Pages Update
The Dodgers continue to play without Andy Pages, as he has been out of action since August 21 with an injury.
MLB.com wrote (on September 15): “Has progressed to hitting baseballs, with the next step being hitting off the Trajekt machine.”
Before getting hurt, Pages had been batting .272 with 134 hits, 21 home runs, 80 RBIs, 72 runs and 12 stolen bases in 128 games.
Looking At Pages
Pages is in the middle of his third season at the MLB level (all with the Dodgers).
He has already helped the Dodgers win two World Series titles (2024-25).
The 25-year-old also made his first career MLB All-Star Game earlier this season.
Looking At The Dodgers Right Now
The Dodgers are in the middle of another outstanding season.
They are at the top of the National League West with a 92-59 record in 151 games.
Over their last ten games, the Dodgers have gone 8-2 (and they are 45-31 in 76 games on the road).
Following their series with the Reds, they will return home to host the San Francisco Giants on Friday night in California.
Looking At The Reds Right Now
The Reds come into the day as the last-place team in the National League Central with a 70-81 record in 151 games.
They have gone 3-7 over their last ten games (and are 36-40 in 76 games at home in Cincinnati).

item.content:encoded:
Josue De Paula received a huge shoutout from one of baseball's biggest stars.
Juan Soto posted a clip of De Paula on his Instagram story, where the Dodgers top prospect was in the midst of working his fifth walk in just four major league games. The New York Mets star called De Paula "el loco mio" on his story as MLB compared the 21-year-old's stance to Soto's.
De Paula and Soto both attended "El Niche" baseball academy in the Dominican Republic. Soto, who had a chance to sign with the Dodgers ahead of the 2025 season, has evidently not lost love for his fellow countryman and budding star.
As for whether De Paula was trying to copy the Soto Shuffle, the Dodgers outfielder explained what was going through his head during that at-bat.
"I wasn't exactly trying to emulate it. It was more just me being so locked in and getting into my legs," he told the California Post Tuesday. "But I can understand how it looks like a Soto shuffle. And if people think it looks like that, hey, I'm not mad at it."
De Paula and Soto have developed a relationship as the pair share representation with Boras Coporation. It appears the former has begun his own version of the Soto Shuffle.
The Dodgers promoted De Paula from Double-A last week to fill in for the injured Shohei Ohtani. Despite being the youngest player in the lineup, De Paula exudes confidence and power when he steps in the batter's box.
Moreover, the De Paula's plate discipline is a rarity for young players. Yet, entering Tuesday night's game he had managed to avoid striking out.
Who else does that remind you of?
Soto.

item.content:encoded:
Mookie Betts and Kiké Hernández wore No. 21 Los Angeles Dodgers jerseys against the Cincinnati Reds on Tuesday night as part of Major League Baseball celebrating Roberto Clemente Day, which is observed every Sept. 15.
MLB permits nominees and previous recipients of the Roberto Clemente Award to wear a No. 21 jersey, and Betts was the winner of last year’s honor. Puerto Rican natives are also allowed to wear the number in honor of Clemente, which Hernández again took advantage of.
Will Smith is the Dodgers’ nominee for this year’s Roberto Clemente Award, and while he did not play in the team’s 4-0 win over the Reds, it also appears he didn’t elect to wear No. 21. Both Betts’ and Hernández’s transaction pages listed them as wearing the number, while Smith’s page still showed him wearing his usual No. 16.
Betts went 0-for-4 with a strikeout against the Reds. Hernández, like Smith, did not appear in the Dodgers’ victory.
The Roberto Clemente Award is presented annually in recognition of the Major League player who best represents the game of baseball through extraordinary character, community involvement, philanthropy and positive contributions, both on and off the field.
The concept of honoring Major League players for their philanthropic work was created in 1971 as the “Commissioner’s Award.” The recognition was renamed to the “Roberto Clemente Award” in 1973 as tribute to Clemente following his passing while delivering relief supplies for earthquake victims in Nicaragua on Dec. 31, 1972.
“I was obviously too young to remember Roberto Clemente, but from the people that I respect and what he was as a person, certainly supersedes what he was as a ballplayer, which says a lot,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said on SportsNet LA.
“Just unfortunately way too young. It’s very cool that young players, current players, understand who Roberto Clemente was and they have that award every year. It’s a big feather in everyone’s cap. Baseball is certainly better with Roberto Clemente.
“I met his family in Pittsburgh, so that was pretty cool. Been to the Roberto Clemente museum in Pittsburgh, which was great for me as well.”
How to vote Will Smith for Roberto Clemente Award
Fans can now vote for the Roberto Clemente Award winner via MLBTogether.com/clementeaward (in both English and Spanish). Fan voting extends through the final day of the regular season on Sunday, Sept. 27. The winner of the fan vote will count as one vote among those cast by the blue-ribbon panel.
The league-wide winner of the Roberto Clemente Award will be honored at the 2026 World Series following selection by the aforementioned panel. It includes representatives from the commissioner’s office, Capital One, MLB-affiliated networks (MLB Network, FOX Sports, ESPN and TBS), MLB.com, National Baseball Hall of Fame, as well as Roberto’s children, Enrique, Luis and Roberto Clemente, Jr.
Smith is looking to become the fifth player in Dodgers franchise history to win the honor. Previous recipients include Betts (2025), Justin Turner (2022), Clayton Kershaw (2012) and Steve Garvey (1981).

Entering Tuesday’s game, Freeman was on a 3-for-30 cold streak and had missed three of the last six games because of his knee issue. Things looked shaky for Freeman, who has built a reputation as one of baseball’s most consistent players. However, he put together his best game in weeks, going 3-for-5 on singles, but showing the elite bat-to-ball sk
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman has been battling right knee pain, but the worst of it may be behind the team’s contact specialist.
Entering Tuesday’s game, Freeman was on a 3-for-30 cold streak and had missed three of the last six games because of his knee issue.
Things looked shaky for Freeman, who has built a reputation as one of baseball’s most consistent players.
However, he put together his best game in weeks, going 3-for-5 on singles, but showing the elite bat-to-ball skills that make him a candidate to bat around .300 year in, year out.
After the game, manager Dave Roberts noted that Freeman looked more like himself.
“It looked good,” Roberts said. “It looked more like Freddie.”
Freeman had asked Roberts before the game, jokingly, if he could play on Wednesday, a scheduled day off, if he got three hits.
As a result of Freeman’s performance, the manager is allowing Freeman to skip an off-day on Wednesday and play again, with the infielder eager to get the ball rolling.
“I feel like my faults are I try to hit the ball to the opposite field too much, and I let the ball get too deep,” he said.
“So today was [get the] foot down early, catch the ball out front a little bit, and it kind of worked. I wasn’t squaring the ball up in the game, but I’ll take those three hits and keep that work going tomorrow, and hopefully we’ll get hot.”
What does Freeman’s uptick mean for the Dodgers?
With the best rotation in baseball, the Dodgers are left scrounging around for offense any way that they can find it.
Teoscar Hernandez, Josue De Paula, and Mookie Betts have been the most consistent sources, with Max Muncy and Will Smith in the picture as well.
Still, the Dodgers need as many players in a spot as possible to deliver timely hits, and Freeman’s experience and skills make him a clear-cut candidate to step up.
To deliver results quickly, as he manages his knee and struggles, Freeman has made a mechanical change, getting out in front of the ball to catch it earlier on his bat.
The result may be less clean contact and hard hits, but more consistent contact, with the idea that it makes him valuable come the postseason.
“I’m not trying to find something that’s sustainable,” he said. “I’m trying to find something that works for four weeks.”
Freeman has the right approach to deliver just what the Dodgers need. The entire offense does not need to be excellent; simply being good enough will lead to a three-peat.

Don’t know when the time of return to play is, but today was positive, and hopefully we can just keep building towards that.” Ohtani has been on the 15-day injured list since Sept.
item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI — Shohei Ohtani hit off a tee in Los Angeles and remains on track to return before the end of the regular season, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said.
“Shohei hit off the tee and felt good, too,” Roberts said. “Don’t know what’s in store for tomorrow, but I know that there’s going to be a consistent build-up. Don’t know when the time of return to play is, but today was positive, and hopefully we can just keep building towards that.”
Ohtani has been on the 15-day injured list since Sept. 8 with right biceps inflammation. His swings were his first since going on the IL.
The four-time MVP is not traveling with the team, but has been working out and getting treatment.
Roberts hopes Ohtani will play in a few more regular-season games. The Dodgers already have clinched a playoff spot.
“Whether it happens or not is to be determined, but I do expect him to be back to play in some regular season games,” Roberts said. “I don’t know how many.”
The magic number for the two-time defending World Series champions to clinch their 13th NL West title in 14 years is down to one.

item.title: [Action News Jax] Report: Robert De Niro negotiating to play Dodgers HOF manager Tommy Lasorda in film

item.description: Two-time Academy Award winner Robert De Niro will portray another legendary sports figure in an upcoming film, according to a published report. De Niro, 83, who won an Oscar for portraying middleweight boxing champion Jake LaMotta in the 1980 film “Raging Bull,” is in talks to play Los Angeles Dodgers Hall of Fame manager Tommy Lasorda, Deadline reported. The film, tentatively called “Tommy and Me,” will be produced by Skydance Sports with Reid Carolin as director, according to the entertainment
item.content:encoded:
Two-time Academy Award winner Robert De Niro will portray another legendary sports figure in an upcoming film, according to a published report.
De Niro, 83, who won an Oscar for portraying middleweight boxing champion Jake LaMotta in the 1980 film “Raging Bull,” is in talks to play Los Angeles Dodgers Hall of Fame manager Tommy Lasorda, Deadline reported.
The film, tentatively called “Tommy and Me,” will be produced by Skydance Sports with Reid Carolin as director, according to the entertainment sports website.
No details have been released about the angle the film will take in depicting the garrulous manager, who “bled Dodger blue” as Los Angeles’ colorful manager from 1976 to 1996.
Lasorda, who compiled a 1,599-2439-3 record with the Dodgers, won four National League pennants and two World Series in Los Angeles. He was inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 1997 by the Veterans Committee.
Lasorda, who died on Jan. 7, 2021, at the age of 93, spent only three seasons in the majors as a left-handed pitcher and had an 0-4 mark. He broke in with the Philadelphia Phillies organization in 1945, but spent the majority of his career as a member of the Dodgers.
He played 11 seasons in the minors for the franchise when it was based in Brooklyn and Los Angeles, and spent 10 season managing Dodger minor leaguers until joining the major league team in 1973 as a third-base coach.
He replaced longtime manager Walter Alston in 1976 and then carved out his own niche as the Dodgers’ skipper, being named N.L. Manager of the Year in 1983 and 1988. He was also the N.L. manager in four All-Star Games.
In addition to “Raging Bull,” De Niro won a Best Supporting Actor Oscar for “The Godfather Part II” as a young Vito Corleone. He has received nine Oscar nominations overall, with other lead actor roles in “Taxi Driver” (1976), “The Deer Hunter” (1978) and “Awakenings” (1990).
De Niro was also nominated for Best Supporting Actor in “Cape Fear” (1991), “Silver Linings Playbook” (2012) and “Killers of the Flower Moon” (2023). He was also nominated for Best Director for the 2019 film “The Irishman.”
The actor also had memorable roles in “Goodfellas” and “Casino.”

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Dodgers' Dave Roberts Says Josue De Paula Needs to Be Better in One Key Area
item.dc:creator: J P Hoornstra; Unknown
