item.content:encoded:
When the Los Angeles Dodgers promoted Josue De Paula to the majors last week, they did so in full knowledge that the 21-year-old had more errors (eight) than assists (six) as a Double-A outfielder.
After playing 58 games in left field and 37 in right field for the Tulsa Drillers, De Paula has spent all but five innings at designated hitter during his first five days in the majors. When he caught the only fly ball hit in his direction over five innings Sunday in Miami, De Paula and the Dodgers could exhale. He got the first one out of the way.
It will be difficult for manager Dave Roberts to take De Paula out of the lineup once Shohei Ohtani returns from the injured list if he continues to reach base at such a high clip.
Yet it will be easier to keep De Paula in the lineup if he can play a corner outfield position. To that end, Roberts is hopeful the rookie can become a better defensive outfielder in short order.
"I just think that — just being candid — I don’t think that he’s valued it as much as he will," Roberts said, via Bill Plunkett of the Orange County Register. "And it just has to be important. Certainly, when you get to the big leagues, outs are important, converting outs are important.
“I think that he’s a young player. I mean, he’s 21 years old. His bat has certainly got him here, but it’s our job to make him value defense and get him to be a better defender.”
Besides their mandate to make De Paula a more complete baseball player, the Dodgers have another pressing reason to get the rookie comfortable in the outfield.
If Ohtani and Dalton Rushing are able to return from the injured list prior to October, they can only occupy the roster as designated hitters or pinch hitters. That's a limiting factor in the postseason, when teams can only carry 26 active players in each round.
De Paula gives the Dodgers three left-handed hitting DHs — impractical at best, impossible at worst — unless he can play the outfield.
"He and Dino [Ebel, the Dodgers' outfielders coach] are committed to a routine, which I love,” Roberts said. “I think the other important thing is just so he can see how the quality and how intense the work is up here. And I think that you really don’t know until you know, and I’m excited for him to watch our guys, how they prepare each night.”

J.P. Hoornstra is an On SI Contributor. A veteran of 20 years of sports coverage for daily newspapers in California, J.P. covered MLB, the Los Angeles Dodgers, and the Los Angeles Angels (occasionally of Anaheim) from 2012-23 for the Southern California News Group. His first book, The 50 Greatest Dodgers Games of All-Time, published in 2015. In 2016, he won an Associated Press Sports Editors award for breaking news coverage. He once recorded a keyboard solo on the same album as two of the original Doors.

Con este triunfo, el conjunto californiano colocó en dos su número mágico para adjudicarse su
item.content:encoded:
Este martes Yoshinobu Yamamoto sumó otro triunfo en la temporada, tras dominar a los Rojos de Cincinnati en el segundo duelo de la serie con blanqueada 4-0. El serpentinero toleró solo un imparable a lo largo de siete episodios para guiar la victoria de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles este martes por la noche, dejando a la escuadrade California a un paso de coronarse en la División Oeste del circuito viejo.
Con este triunfo, el conjunto californiano colocó en dos su número mágico para adjudicarse su decimotercer banderín divisional en los últimos catorce años. Tras sellar su clasificación a la postemporada el pasado lunes, Los Ángeles continúa en la pelea por la cima de la Liga Nacional.
Lee también: Astros pierden a Carlos Correa por lesión
Yamamoto quien cuenta con récord de 14-8 completó salida número 27 de la campaña (líder dentro del cuerpo de pitcheo del equipo) con efectividad de 2.67 en la temporada regular de 2026.
Posterior a ese batazo, el diestro retiró en fila a diez adversarios, concedió un par de pasaportes y recetó siete ponches. Es la segunda jornada consecutiva en la que un abridor de la tropa de California firma una labor de siete entradas en blanco, emulando lo hecho por Tarik Skubal el día anterior.
El cuerpo de serpentineros de los Dodgers firmó su blanqueada número 12 de la zafra, mientras que la ofensiva de los Rojos se quedó sin anotar por decimoséptima ocasión en el torneo.
Calma para los ajustes
Tras el encuentro el serpentinero japonés aseguró a la prensa: «Bueno, al principio no tenía muy buen control de mis sensaciones o mi mecánica, por lo que estuve un poco fuera de zona con la pelota. Pero mantuve la calma y la compostura, y fui capaz de hacer los ajustes a tiempo», expresó.
Tarik Skubal en el duelo anterior sentenció la victoria también por blanqueo en el primer duelo de la serie, sobre esto Yamamoto destacó que esa actuación lo animó a ser más firme en los pitcheos.
«Lo que hizo (Tarik Skubal) el lunes me dio una imagen muy positiva antes del encuentro de este martes. Me animó a ser agresivo y a atacar a los bateadores», dijo.

item.content:encoded:
“Bateó desde el ‘tee’ y se sintió bien”: Shohei Ohtani hace sus primeros swings desde que se lesionó
La estrella japonesa no está viajando con el equipo.
PUBLICIDAD
Cincinnati. Shohei Ohtani bateó desde un tee el martes en Los Ángeles y sigue encaminado a regresar antes de que termine la temporada regular, manifestó el mánager de los Dodgers, Dave Roberts.
“Shohei bateó desde el tee y también se sintió bien”, comentó Roberts. “No sé qué nos depara mañana, pero sé que habrá una progresión constante. No sé cuándo será el momento de volver a jugar, pero hoy fue positivo y ojalá podamos seguir avanzando hacia eso”.
Ohtani ha estado en la lista de lesionados de 15 días desde el 8 de septiembre por una inflamación en el bíceps derecho. Los swings del martes fueron los primeros desde que ingresó en la lista de lesionados.
El cuatro veces Jugador Más Valioso no está viajando con el equipo, pero ha estado entrenando y recibiendo tratamiento.
Roberts espera que Ohtani juegue en algunos partidos más de la temporada regular. Los Dodgers ya aseguraron un puesto en los playoffs.
“Que ocurra o no está por verse, pero sí espero que regrese para jugar algunos partidos de la temporada regular. No sé cuántos”, señaló el piloto.
Los dos veces campeones defensores de la Serie Mundial llegaron al juego del martes por la noche en Cincinnati con un número mágico de tres para asegurar su decimotercer título del Oeste de la Liga Nacional en 14 años.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Edwin Diaz Dealt Bad News on Future With Los Angeles Dodgers
item.dc:creator: Dibyendu Mondal
item.description: Edwin Diaz signed a three-year, $69 million contract in December. It made him baseball's highest-paid reliever by average annual salary. His first season for the Los Angeles Dodgers has not matched that price tag. Diaz opened the year on a rocky note. He allowed one run through his first five outings. Two rough appearances followed. Doctors then found loose bodies in his right elbow. He had arthroscopic surgery and missed roughly 100 days. He returned in late July and posted mixed results. The D
item.content:encoded:
Edwin Diaz signed a three-year, $69 million contract in December. It made him baseball's highest-paid reliever by average annual salary. His first season for the Los Angeles Dodgers has not matched that price tag.
Diaz opened the year on a rocky note. He allowed one run through his first five outings. Two rough appearances followed.
Doctors then found loose bodies in his right elbow. He had arthroscopic surgery and missed roughly 100 days.
He returned in late July and posted mixed results. The Dodgers placed him back on the injured list Aug. 18. This time, doctors diagnosed inflammation on the right side of his neck.
Diaz has an 11.85 ERA in 16 appearances this season. He has thrown 13 2/3 innings for the Los Angeles Dodgers. The right-hander has struck out 19 batters and walked 10.
That uneven form has created real uncertainty about his spot on the postseason roster.
Edwin Diaz's Roster Spot Now in Doubt
insider Ken Rosenthal addressed Diaz's situation on the show "Foul Territory." He said the Dodgers will pick their 26 best players, regardless of salary.
The club has called this year's pitching staff its deepest ever heading into October.
Rosenthal added that if evaluators view Diaz as not good enough, the Dodgers will leave him off. Rosenthal called it a "win-at-all-costs kind of industry."
Manager Dave Roberts has not guaranteed Diaz a spot either. "We have to go with our best pitchers," Roberts said. Diaz has not pitched well enough yet during his rehab assignment.
He allowed five runs while recording two outs in his Sept. 13 outing. He is set for another rehab appearance Sept. 16, with an expected return in late September.
The stakes are real. The Dodgers clinched a playoff berth Monday with a win over the Cincinnati Reds.
Latest Updates on Edwin Diaz, Shohei Ohtani
The Dodgers updated their injury report this week. Several key players remain sidelined heading into the stretch run.
Diaz remains on the 15-day injured list with neck inflammation. He is on a rehab assignment with Triple-A Oklahoma City.
Shohei Ohtani is on the 15-day injured list with a left knee and right biceps injury, retroactive to Sept. 8. He could return as a hitter as soon as Sept. 23. He is not expected to pitch again until 2027. He began a swing progression Sept. 15, hitting off a tee.
Outfielder Andy Pages has a fractured left hand. He landed on the 10-day injured list Aug. 22. He has progressed to hitting baseballs off a machine, with an expected return in late September as well.

item.title: [Friars on Base] Padres hoping Edwin Díaz makes Dodgers' playoff roster as struggles reach breaking point
item.dc:creator: PJ Potter
item.description: It has been a nightmare season for three-time Reliever of the Year Edwin Díaz. In his first year with the Los Angeles Dodgers, he's made two trips to the injured list, all while logging a -1.3 bWAR and 11.85 ERA. The Dodgers were hoping that Díaz would help cement a third straight World Series title, but considering every bit of struggle from the 32-year-old closer, they may keep him off the postseason roster if no sign of progress is being made. “We have to go with our best pitchers, as far as
item.content:encoded:
It has been a nightmare season for three-time Reliever of the Year Edwin Díaz. In his first year with the Los Angeles Dodgers, he's made two trips to the injured list, all while logging a -1.3 bWAR and 11.85 ERA.
The Dodgers were hoping that Díaz would help cement a third straight World Series title, but considering every bit of struggle from the 32-year-old closer, they may keep him off the postseason roster if no sign of progress is being made.
“We have to go with our best pitchers, as far as performance, talent, all that stuff,” Roberts said in The Athletic's report. “So my bet is that he will be (on the roster). But again, there’s got to be some kind of evidence or something for us, again, to sort of bet on. And so my bet is yes, but we still got to see something.”
The San Diego Padres, among every other National League postseason hopeful, are crossing their fingers that the Dodgers ultimately keep Díaz on the roster.
Padres fans can finally point to a Dodgers' problem with merit
For the last few seasons, it felt like the Dodgers were invincible. Seemingly every MVP and All-Star joined the organization, conjuring up a super team that has baseball fans worried about a potential lockout this upcoming offseason.
So for once, San Diego fans can actually look at Los Angeles and smile as they hold an advantage over them. The Padres have a much better closer, and it's not even close to being an argument anymore.
Mason Miller's 1.12 ERA, 0.855 WHIP, and league-best 37 saves make the Padres that much better of a contending playoff team. The Dodgers can't say about their closer anymore. In a rehab stint this past Sunday with Triple-A Oklahoma City, Díaz was torched for five runs in 0.2 innings against minor leaguers, surrendering three walks and two hits.
Entering Tuesday's games, the Padres would face the Dodgers in the NLDS if they were to advance out of the Wild Card round. The Friars, and their fans, are hoping that Dodgers feel forced to have Díaz on the postseason roster.
After all, he is getting paid $60 million by Los Angeles over the next three seasons. He's not the easiest guy to part with.

Yamamoto (14-8) picked up the win in Tuesday's 4-0 victory over the Reds, allowing one hit and two walks over seven scoreless innings. He struck out seven.
The right-hander uncharacteristically walked the first two batters he faced, but Yamamoto would only let one other batter reach base before exiting after 91 pitches (55 strikes). The quality start was his 21st of the season, tied for the major-league lead with the Marlins' Sandy Alcantara, and over 10 starts since the All-Star break, Yamamoto has reeled off a 1.98 ERA, 0.79 WHIP and 72:16 K:BB in 68.1 innings. He'll look to keep rolling in what will likely be his final outing of the regular season, at home early next week against the Padres.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yoshinobu Yamamoto Shows Dodgers Exactly Why He Should Start Game 1
item.dc:creator: Nelson Espinal
item.description: When he needed it most, starter Yoshinobu Yamamoto reminded everyone in the Los Angeles Dodgers clubhouse why he is the man for Game 1 of any playoff series. A day after the Dodgers clinched their postseason berth and secured a shot at completing their three-peat, Yamamoto took the mound to help the team in their postseason seeding race with a road game against the Cincinnati Reds on Wednesday, September 16th. Yamamoto went seven scoreless innings, allowing one hit and two walks while getting ei
item.content:encoded:
When he needed it most, starter Yoshinobu Yamamoto reminded everyone in the Los Angeles Dodgers clubhouse why he is the man for Game 1 of any playoff series.
A day after the Dodgers clinched their postseason berth and secured a shot at completing their three-peat, Yamamoto took the mound to help the team in their postseason seeding race with a road game against the Cincinnati Reds on Wednesday, September 16th.
Yamamoto went seven scoreless innings, allowing one hit and two walks while getting eight punchouts, and looked like he had much more in the tank.
Manager Dave Roberts could have easily kept Yamamoto in for at least another inning; the Japanese pitcher had only 91 pitches down, given his propensity to pitch a high volume.
He allowed only two hard hits, highlighting his dominance, and both walks came on his first two batters.
Yamamoto retired 21 of the final 22 batters he faced, threw 16 whiffs, and used a wide variety of pitches, with none exceeding 25% usage.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto had another great outing, his best one in a while:
7 IP
1 H
2 BB
7 Ks
He looked great and could have gone another inning on just 91 pitches.
Quick and efficient from the Dodgers' ace. pic.twitter.com/pro7lpwsiK
The outing was a nice change of pace for Yamamoto, who has been prone to the long ball and giving up hard contact.
Instead, he did a good job of keeping the Reds hitters off-balance, and it looked like what Dodger fans have come to expect from Yamamoto: efficiency, elite pitch mix, and weak contact.
Why Dave Roberts Trusts Yamamoto
More than anything, his ability to move on from mistakes, like his lack of command that led to two walks right off the bat, is really the special sauce for Yamamoto.
Roberts, after the game, spoke to this resilience and how it translates perfectly to October and high-leverage moments, when everyone gets tested in some shape or fashion.
"I think the thing that I've learned about Yoshinobu is he's able to reset on the fly," the skipper said.
"He's able to bear down and make pitches when he needs to, to get a double play, a strikeout, a pop-up.
"Those are separators. When you're not totally locked in or in sync, you can still take a deep breath, reset, and navigate an inning and keep going. And so that's something that I've really learned from him."
Why Yamamoto Needed This Outing Now
Given his 2025 postseason exploits, it is hard to argue that Yamamoto has much to prove in the playoffs, and he needs to make his case to pitch the first game in the postseason.
Pitching in Game 1, when the team is fully healthy, is the ultimate nod of respect for an ace, and earning that honor as a member of his special rotation makes it all the more noteworthy.
Yamamoto, given his track record, has seemingly been in pole position all season, but Blake Snell's form and Tarik Skubal's arrival have sparked a healthy debate about who takes the ball first.
Since returning from the IL after elbow surgery on August 11th, Snell has a 1.04 ERA through 34.2 innings. He has 46 strikeouts and 14 walks in that span.
Yamamoto has a 1.98 ERA in 68.1 innings since the All-Star break. His ratio is 72 strikeouts to 16 walks.
By comparison, Skubal has a 2.52 ERA in 50 innings with the Dodgers since joining from the trade deadline on August 3rd. He also has a 57 strikeouts-to-11 walks ratio.
Recently, Skubal had his own seven-inning scoreless outing, and he looked very settled in, while Snell has not put a foot wrong.
However, Yamamoto's latest outing showed the front office that he can deliver a vintage Yamamoto outing, which, come postseason time, is invaluable.
It means he can provide a long outing, sometimes a complete game, along with minimal runs allowed, and leave the hitters in a tizzy.

item.title: [CBS Sports] Blake Snell, Dodgers look to clinch NL West title against Reds

Left-hander Blake Snell (4-1, 1.91 ERA) will return to Great American Ball Park, where he no-hit the Cincinnati Reds on Aug. 2, 2024, as a member of the San Francisco Giants. Now with the Dodgers, the veteran southpaw will look to create that magic again as Los Angele
item.content:encoded:
With a chance to clinch their 13th division title in 14 straight playoff seasons, the Los Angeles Dodgers will start a pitcher who threw a no-hitter in his most recent start on the mound he will be on Wednesday night in Cincinnati.
Left-hander Blake Snell (4-1, 1.91 ERA) will return to Great American Ball Park, where he no-hit the Cincinnati Reds on Aug. 2, 2024, as a member of the San Francisco Giants. Now with the Dodgers, the veteran southpaw will look to create that magic again as Los Angeles positions itself for a deep postseason run.
That night in 2024, Snell struck out 11 and walked three in San Francisco's 3-0 win, which concluded when Elly De La Cruz flied out to right-center. Snell will face Cincinnati for the first time since he started Game 1 of the National League wild-card series last season, holding Cincinnati to two runs and four hits over seven innings of a 10-5 win for host Los Angeles. Snell struck out nine and walked one.
The two-time Cy Young Award winner has completed at least five innings and hasn't allowed more than one earned run in each of his six starts since his return from May arthroscopic surgery, which removed loose bodies in his left elbow. He has allowed a total of just four runs and has 46 strikeouts across 34 2/3 innings and has a 4-0 record and 1.04 ERA since then.
The 33-year-old veteran struck out eight, walked two and allowed four hits and one run over 5 2/3 innings in his most recent start, a 6-2 victory last Friday against the Miami Marlins.
"I think I can be way better," Snell said. "I think it's going good because just pitching in this league so much, I understand hitters, and I'm starting to adjust quicker, which I'm getting excited about. I go out there with a plan and being able to adjust and get quick outs off of that, or get ahead to get strikeouts. It's starting to get quicker, which I'm extremely happy about."
The Dodgers (92-59) have won all five meetings with the Reds this season and are trying to catch the Milwaukee Brewers (94-57) for the best overall record in the major leagues this season.
Also, a Dodgers win or a San Diego Padres loss on Wednesday would clinch the fifth straight NL West title for the Dodgers, who have champagne waiting for them outside the visitors' clubhouse in Cincinnati.
The mood is much different for the Reds (70-81), who lost 4-0 to the Dodgers on Tuesday following a 4-1 loss in the opener of a four-game series on Monday. Tuesday's shutout was the Reds' 17th of the season. Cincinnati has dropped seven of its past eight games to fall to a season-low 11 games below .500.
The Reds on Wednesday will send a left-hander of their own to the mound in Andrew Abbott (6-11, 4.78 ERA), making his career-high 31st start of the season. It has been a volatile campaign for the 27-year-old Abbott, who has given up 24 home runs and has only 11 quality starts.
Abbott is coming off a nightmarish outing against the Milwaukee Brewers on Friday. He was tagged for eight runs (seven earned) on nine hits in just two innings during a 20-0 blowout loss.
"The only good thing I did was throw strikes, but I was in the zone too much," Abbott said. "I let the team down by getting yanked in the second after such a bad start. That didn't feel good."
De La Cruz had two of Cincinnati's three hits on Tuesday and has an MLB-leading 22-game on-base streak.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers recently sent Edwin Díaz on his second rehab assignment of the season. His first stint in Oklahoma City — back when he was rehabbing following elbow surgery — didn't go well. He posted a 10.80 ERA in just 1⅓ innings. Impossibly, however, he's been even worse his second time around.
Díaz has made four rehab outings for the so far. His first was almost spotless (he gave up a walk), but his second lasted just ⅔ innings after he gave up a run on two walks. The third was a promising bounce back — one hit, one walk, no earned runs in a full inning — but his latest was a downright disaster.
On Sunday, Diaz gave up five earned runs on two hits, a hit by pitch, and three walks. He was yanked before he could get out of the inning.
The Dodgers still have a few days before they need to make a roster move, but under no circumstances can he be used in close games, not even if they clinch a postseason berth. The Atlanta Braves are still within striking distance for a first-round bye, and the Dodgers can't afford to lose it.
When Díaz comes back, the only acceptable situation to use him in would be a blowout, and even then, fans would find it impossible to trust him. Although Tanner Scott appears to be turning back into a pumpkin, even he would lend the team greater reassurances in close games.
Edwin Díaz's latest rehab meltdown should force Dodgers to leave him off their postseason roster
It also puts the Dodgers in an uncomfortable but undeniable position: Díaz can't be on the postseason roster.
Roki Sasaki is likely to go back to the rotation when he returns from injury, but repeating his role as LA's lights-out postseason closer could be on the docket if Scott fails to prove himself trustworthy. Tyler Glasnow is also expected to move to the bullpen in October, so the Dodgers could even audition him in the role.
While the Dodgers are still the heavy favorites to win the World Series, it'll be an undeniable embarrassment to the team if they do it without Díaz — their $69 million man — who they haven't been able to figure out all season long.

item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers clinched a postseason spot for the 14th consecutive season and are closing in on a 13th National League West title during that span. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers clinched a postseason spot for the 14th consecutive season and are closing in on a 13th National League West title during that span.
Also of importance for the Dodgers is finishing with a top two record in the NL as it would come with a first-round bye in the playoffs. That could be of particular value to a slew of injured Dodgers, including Shohei Ohtani, Andy Pages, Dalton Rushing and Edgardo Henriquez.
Dodgers updates
Dalton Rushing
Rushing made a surprising return on Sept. 1 from a slight tear in the UCL of his right elbow, but only managed to appear in four games off the bench before going back on the 10-day injured list. That came after Rushing was scratched from the lineup due to right elbow trouble that stemmed from his attempt at a throwing progression.
The Dodgers have since ruled out Rushing possibly catching again this year, but they remain hopeful he will be an option as a left-handed bat off the bench.
“Dalton’s doing well,” manager Dave Roberts said on SportsNet LA. “Building up his progression.”
Shohei Ohtani
Ohtani started his swinging progression on Tuesday by hitting off a tee. Roberts said he “felt good” doing so and is going to continue moving along.
“I don’t know what’s in store for tomorrow, but I know there’s going to be a consistent buildup. Don’t know when the time to return to play is, but today was positive and hopefully we can just keep building toward that,” Roberts said.
Roberts added he believes Ohtani will return at some point in the regular season, but cautioned, “Whether it happens or not is to be determined.”
Ohtani is eligible to be activated off the 15-day injured list Sept. 23.
Andy Pages
Pages has been swinging a bat for several days and took a step forward on Tuesday by hitting off pitching machine. Next for Pages is to log at-bats against the Trajekt machine.
Edgardo Henriquez
Henriquez, the latest Dodgers injury, returned to Los Angeles in order to undergo testing on his back/side area. He was officially put on the 15-day injured list due to low back discomfort, but Roberts noted there might be some trouble with the oblique as well.
Henriquez is not eligible to return during the regular season but the Dodgers hope he will be available for the playoffs.
Have you subscribed to the Dodger Blue YouTube channel? Be sure to ring the notification bell to watch player interviews, participate in shows and giveaways, and stay up to date on all Dodgers news and rumors!

item.content:encoded:
The other day I walked outside my apartment in New York and noticed the slightest hint of a chill in the morning air. And I could only think of one thing: the postseason is almost here. The long baseball season is drawing to a close. The delight of October awaits.
And then …
Oh, yeah. The lockout.
The next few months could reshape the future of baseball. I suppose we shall see how it goes. Until then, let’s take some questions. As always, they have been edited for clarity.
Advertisement
Which wild-card team has the best chance to upset a division winner? — bbrathizza2075
There are a lot of worthy candidates, especially in the National League. But I would have to say the Yankees, if only because on paper, the Yankees should be the best team in the American League, even if they are unlikely to catch the American League East. The Yankees lead the AL in run differential by a significant margin. No AL lineup has hit more home runs. In Cam Schlittler, they employ the Cy Young favorite. And they still have Aaron Judge.
So the Yankees would be my pick, but the talent on the other wild-card clubs is immense. The Phillies can line up Cristopher Sánchez, Zack Wheeler and, if he’s healthy, Jesús Luzardo in a five-game series. Good luck. Pete Crow-Armstrong has been the best player in baseball for a Cubs team that boasts the best offense in baseball. A healthy Nick Pivetta provides San Diego with enough rotation stability for a short series, in which their bullpen would be hellish to face. And the Padres, who would likely face the Dodgers, have shown a willingness in recent years to stand and trade blows with baseball’s reigning champs.
And, really, what qualifies as an upset? If the 98-win Rays lose to the 94-win Yankees in a five-game series, would it really be shocking? Same story with the Phillies or the Cubs facing the Brewers. These teams will be quite evenly matched. It should be an entertaining October.
Which National League fanbase would be MOST disappointed if its team doesn’t hoist the commissioner’s trophy in 2026? Big narrative-ball postseason for Brewers, Phillies and even Cubs fans in my opinion. — Jacob N.
I think it’s a toss-up between Milwaukee and Philadelphia. And I would lean toward the Phillies.
When it comes to the Brewers, a lot of folks in baseball have asked the question: If not now, when? Well, the team made clear, in part by declining to go bonkers and acquire Tarik Skubal, that it rejects the premise. And the Brewers brain trust may be wise to do so. This team is well-situated to contend in 2026, but also well beyond 2026. Jackson Chourio is 22. Jacob Misiorowski is 24. Logan Henderson is 24. Brice Turang is practically ancient at 26. Jesús Made and Luis Peña are on the way. This team isn’t going anywhere.
Right. Right?
Well …
Baltimore fans felt the same way after a 101-win campaign in 2023. Instead, they’ve watched the Orioles degrade from budding juggernaut into a last-place club. And while I do not foresee that fate for the Brewers, it remains within the realm of possibility. Misiorowski may not stay healthy beyond this season. The 2026 campaign could be this group’s best chance to win the first championship in franchise history.
Advertisement
Even so, I don’t think the psychological blow of an early exit would sting Brewers fans like it would Phillies fans. There is just so much frustration stored up within that fanbase, dating to that shocking collapse in the 2023 National League Championship Series. There are also legitimate questions about how long the window will remain open for this group. Again, it comes back to age. Kyle Schwarber is 33. Bryce Harper turns 34 in October. Zack Wheeler is 36. Trea Turner is playing below-replacement-level at 33 — and his contract will not expire until 2033. The farm system has not produced much in recent years, and Dave Dombrowski has not done well on the free-agent market.
So while Brewers fans may be infuriated about the unfairness of MLB’s system, and while they may lament another missed opportunity, they can credibly believe they will have another shot in 2027. That is harder to fathom for Phillies fans.
The first two teams to clinch playoff berths were the Rays and Brewers. Could you shed any light on the Tampa Bay model both teams adhere to? — Gary D.
Back in 2021, I wrote a lengthy feature about the Rays and their ruthless roster building. The simplest way to describe it is they make a lot of transactions, and that churning allows them to occasionally unearth stars.
Here is one example. Back in 2008, the Rays chose Tim Beckham with the first overall pick in the draft. Beckham was essentially a bust. He took five years to reach the majors and never really hit. In 2017, after nearly a decade of trying to develop him, Tampa Bay dealt Beckham to Baltimore for minor-league pitcher Tobias Myers. He spent a few seasons in Tampa Bay’s farm system before getting traded to Cleveland for a teenage prospect from the Dominican Republic. You may have heard of him by now: Junior Caminero. And Caminero has become the sort of star the Rays once envisioned Beckham could have been. The team turned a failure into a smashing success.
Now, most front offices don’t get a decade to oversee decisions like this. Andrew Friedman was in charge when Beckham was drafted. Chaim Bloom was running the show when Beckham was traded. And Erik Neander, who has worked in the organization since 2007, was the head of baseball operations for the Caminero deal. But the organizational ethos hasn’t changed all that much over the past decade.
Advertisement
Milwaukee also tends toward roster churn but is a tad less aggressive than Tampa Bay. The Brewers are run by Rays alum Matt Arnold, and that man does love a three-team trade. They can find great production on the margins, as they have this season with Jake Bauers. And they are unafraid to deal star players as their contracts expire, as they did in recent years with Corbin Burnes, Devin Williams and Freddy Peralta. Where Milwaukee really excels is scouting Latin America. It signed Chourio and outfielder Luis Lara out of Venezuela. They signed Made and Peña out of the Dominican.
These are the things that small-market teams would like to emulate. Do well in the draft. Don’t stay static on the margins of the roster. And excel in finding stars out of the international market. If it was easy, every team would do it.
Do you think we have seen the last of Shohei Ohtani as a pitcher/starter? — Tae K.
I do not. He will pitch again. But how the Dodgers deploy him will be fascinating.
Multiple things can be true:
1. Shohei Ohtani might be the best pitcher in the world.
He demonstrated that during his 14 starts this season. He posted a 1.79 ERA while striking out 10 batters per nine innings. And he did that while toting the responsibility of batting leadoff as the designated hitter most days in between outings. He looked, in a word, awesome.
2. As he enters his mid-30s, Ohtani probably cannot complete a full season as a two-way player.
The basic story of Ohtani’s professional life is people within baseball telling him, “Hey! You can’t do that,” and Ohtani responding, “Well, actually, I can.” But Father Time is undefeated, and Ohtani has learned that the two-way load is far tougher to shoulder at 32 than it was at 27. He is currently on the injured list dealing with problems with his neck, knee and biceps. And there may be other maladies the famously private Ohtani has not revealed. Suffice to say, he is quite banged up, and no one within the Dodgers organization is thrilled about the situation.
Advertisement
These two facts — Ohtani’s greatness and his fallibility — present the Dodgers with a conflict. There is a clear compromise: the team should ask him to spend the first half of the season as a hitter and then use the second half to build up arm strength so he can be available to pitch in October. Problem solved!
Well, not exactly. Ohtani has agency in this situation. He may not want to give up the full-season two-way dream so easily. He may still want to prove that he can do in his 30s what he did in his 20s. He may still want to say, “Well, actually, I can.” And the Dodgers may not want to scuffle with the face of the franchise. It will be a delicate dance.
How Ohtani feels about his future is unclear. He has not spoken to reporters since Sept. 7, and did not accompany the club on its current trip to Miami and Cincinnati. But he has been staunch his entire career about wanting to remain a two-way player. “The reason why I’m a two-way player is because that’s who I am,” he said during the 2025 postseason. “And it’s what I can do.”
I still think he can be a two-way player, and I would be shocked if he tried to only hit moving forward. But the prospect of him being a healthy two-way player over the course of a 162-game season feels more like a fantasy than a reality. Then again, Ohtani has shown us, over and over in his career, that he can make dreams come true.
Catchers were the overwhelming best at ABS challenges, but I am curious how they fared at challenging as batters compared to batters at other positions. — Anonymous
Interesting premise.
I looked this up and found essentially no correlation. Now, there may be a connection, because while I am not a math wizard, I don’t think one unfinished season provides enough data for a sufficient sample size. At least this year, there is little evidence that, as hitters, catchers perform better than other hitters with ABS.
Dillon Dingler entered Monday’s games rated as the best challenger among catchers, according to FanGraphs. But as a hitter? Dingler graded below average. Same story for Hunter Goodman and J.T. Realmuto, the two catchers rated best behind Dingler.
Among the hitters, there were two catchers rated in Savant’s top 10 for ABS efficiency: Tyler Stephenson and Gabriel Moreno. Iván Herrera came in at No. 14. But then no catcher appears on the leaderboard until Brandon Valenzuela at No. 34. So, like I said, interesting premise, but no real correlation that this knucklehead who flunked geometry in high school can find.
Advertisement
For the last couple of decades, Major League Baseball has seemed to have a major “household name” gap with the NBA and NFL, and Rob Manfred once addressed this by complaining that Mike Trout wasn’t doing more to make himself famous. How is the league working to grow its fanbase and promote its product? — Alex R.
The owners are planning to lock out the players when the collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1.
What are your most realistic thoughts on the lockout? — pollrobb
When I talk to people in baseball about the lockout, they usually say some version of the same thing: they really don’t know what will happen, but they think it will be bad. The negotiations will be contentious. The rhetoric will be vicious. They may well miss games.
My guess — and I will repeat that this is a guess — is that the lockout resolves at some point in March, with enough time to cram a 162-game season into the calendar, in a result similar to the last lockout. I do not foresee the players caving and accepting a salary cap. But it is also hard to identify, in that scenario, what would trigger the owners to stop pushing for one. Genuinely, I do not know how it will go, and anyone who tells you they do is probably overselling their insight.
Why would the players and league not work on solving 100 small things in negotiation now and figure out the big topic at the end? Is it really going to wreck what they have while fighting over billions of dollars? I truly enjoy the game and can’t believe they say it can all wait until December, so they can blame each other. Why not now? — Lynn Z.
To be fair, the two sides have traded a variety of proposals on issues besides the salary cap. They are negotiating. But the small stuff is small for a reason. And the big thing — the potential implementation of a salary cap — is much bigger than anything on the table in the previous round of negotiations. For the owners, the possibility of a cap means billions of dollars gained in franchise values. But for the players, accepting a cap means the collapse of the free-market system that the union has fought so strenuously to maintain for decades. These are existential questions for both sides. And neither side will be inclined to budge until the calendar flips into 2027 and spring training draws closer. So, buckle up. It is going to be a long, bumpy ride.

item.content:encoded:
Robert De Niro está en conversaciones para interpretar a Tommy Lasorda, el emblemático entrenador de los Dodgers que falleció en 2021, en un biopic que prepara Skydance Sports. Lasorda, una figura histórica del béisbol, estuvo asociado a los Dodgers durante más de siete décadas, primero como jugador y luego como entrenador.
Según señala Deadline, citando fuentes cercanas a la producción, el título provisional de la película es Tommy & Me. La dirección estará a cargo de Reid Carolin, conocido por trabajos como Magic Mike y Dog. Un viaje salvaje, quien también firma el guion junto a George Gallo y Cambron Clark. Aunque todavía no se han revelado detalles específicos sobre el enfoque narrativo del filme, Carolin también estará a cargo de la producción a través de Free Association, compañía que lidera junto a Channing Tatum. Entre sus próximos proyectos, Carolin dirigirá Isle of Man, un drama deportivo sobre carreras de motos.
En cuanto a De Niro, el reconocido actor ganador de dos premios Oscar, tiene pendiente el estreno de Ahora los suegros son ellos el próximo 27 de septiembre. Tommy & Me sería su segundo biopic tras su interpretación en Toro salvaje, película que le valió la estatuilla a mejor actor principal en 1981.
Lasorda mantuvo durante 71 años una relación con los Dodgers, siendo la más duradera en la historia del equipo
Nacido en Pensilvania y descendiente de inmigrantes italianos, Lasorda inició su trayectoria en el béisbol profesional al firmar con los Philadelphia Phillies en 1945. En 1949, debutó en las ligas menores con los Brooklyn Dodgers, aunque solo jugó como titular en un encuentro. Su carrera como jugador se caracterizó por las dificultades, pero su verdadero legado comenzó a construirse tras retirarse como jugador.
En 1960, tras la creación de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, se unió al equipo como ojeador. En 1973, el entonces entrenador, Walter Alston, lo incorporó como entrenador de tercera base con miras a que eventualmente lo sucediera. Finalmente, cuatro años después, cuando Alston se retiró, Lasorda tomó las riendas del equipo.
Durante dos décadas al frente de los Dodgers, Lasorda logró cuatro títulos de la Liga Nacional y dos campeonatos de la Serie Mundial. En sus últimos años, continuó como asesor del equipo, involucrándose en la formación de nuevos talentos y asistiendo a entrenamientos. Además, era habitual verle en el Dodger Stadium como espectador, siempre cerca del banquillo que ocupó como entrenador.

item.title: [The New York Times] ‘I just want to feel saucy’: Inside Josue De Paula’s fearless Dodgers debut

item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI — Josue De Paula is in his element in the batter’s box. He carries himself like a guy who knows his importance to the Los Angeles Dodgers depends on how well he can command himself within those 24 square feet of chalk lines. De Paula asserts himself with a confident shake of the head after each pitch outside the strike zone.
Advertisement
Some head shakes are more exaggerated than others. Each demonstrates the same message: De Paula is not going to give in.
“I just want to feel saucy when I’m up there, you know what I’m saying?” De Paula told The Athletic this week. “I feel like I’m in control, not you. … I want my pitch. Come in the zone. Let’s go.”
This is who De Paula wants to be. He describes hitting as “aggressive patience,” an approach that puts him on the attack.
“It’s almost like a war for me in my head,” De Paula said. “I look confident. I look saucy. I feel saucy when I’m in the box, so it’s like, ‘Hey bro, let’s keep it rocking.’”
It took four games for De Paula to inspire fascination within the Dodgers dynasty, where his every at-bat feels like a must-watch example of how to command a zone. Of the first 37 big-league pitches De Paula saw outside of the strike zone, he swung at just five. He made it 17 plate appearances without striking out before going down swinging in the seventh inning and looking in the ninth in the Dodgers’ 4-0 win over the Reds on Tuesday. De Paula does not seem fazed that he is just 2 for 14 (.143) since being called up, including five hitless at-bats in his first game in the leadoff spot.
That’s because he believes in his process. A day earlier, De Paula battled back from down in the count against Reds lefty Nick Lodolo, a former All-Star. The left-handed batter took a 2-2 fastball just below the knees, crouched and shook his head. A pitch later, De Paula walked for the fifth time in his short career.
The clip of the head shake drew a chuckle from the proprietor of the “Soto Shuffle” himself, Juan Soto, who, like De Paula, once honed his craft at the El Niche Baseball Academy in the Dominican city of Santo Domingo.
Josue De Paula live reaction to you trying to get him to chase. https://t.co/CrmRSnDVgO pic.twitter.com/dbXGz8WYL0
— Chad Moriyama (@ChadMoriyama) September 14, 2026
“El loco mío,” Soto shared to his Instagram story in Spanish, stamping his approval with a laughing emoji. My guy.
Advertisement
“I swear I wasn’t trying to do like the whole thing,” De Paula said with a laugh. “I just got into my legs, and I was shaking my head … but I’m not mad. That’s not a bad player to look like.”
De Paula, 21, feels like an injection of youthful exuberance for baseball’s oldest lineup. The Brooklyn-born son of a Dominican father (and relative of NBA veterans Stephon Marbury and Sebastian Telfair) speaks with a thick New York accent and oozes the confidence of a player who carries that swagger into the box.
De Paula is the crown jewel of a Dodgers farm system that is expected to prolong this run of excellence. Last week, he became the first position player ever to be called up directly from Double A by this Andrew Friedman-led front office group.
De Paula is here because he can hit, has always hit, and the Dodgers need him to hit. De Paula is here to serve as the Dodgers’ designated hitter, at least until Shohei Ohtani returns from the injured list. No one with the Dodgers, however, is ruling out the possibility that De Paula could help them in October as they seek a third consecutive World Series title.
“I hope he makes our decision hard,” manager Dave Roberts said.
Through De Paula’s torrid run through the Dodgers’ farm system, officials raved about his keen ability to pick up the baseball, make proper swing decisions and recognize spin.
“He doesn’t give away any pitches, which I love, let alone give away any at-bats,” Roberts said.
Pair that with a preternatural ability to make contact, and De Paula entered this season as one of the highly-regarded young hitters in the league. The Dodgers implemented a change to De Paula’s swing this year, lowering his hands and opening up his resulting bat path to keep the barrel in the zone longer. That has allowed him to access more power by pulling more fly balls and has made him a lethal producer at Double A.
Advertisement
De Paula slugged 27 home runs this season in Double A, more than double what he had in any of his first four professional seasons. His first hit Sunday in Miami was a mammoth upper-deck shot to right field on the kind of awe-inspiring swing that has come much more easily for De Paula than in years past.
“When all those things are kind of clicking, it’s tough for any pitcher to compete with,” hitting coach Robert Van Scoyoc said. “So it’s been very impressive so far.”
De Paula became a Dodger partially as a byproduct of the COVID-19 pandemic, which shut down the New York baseball season and prompted De Paula’s father, Josue Sr., to send him to the Dominican Republic to work at El Niche under Cristian “Niche” Batista.
“It was like stepping into a whole other world,” De Paula said.
It was there, during an offseason workout, that De Paula met Soto, who broke into the big leagues at 19 years old with the kind of swaggering command of the batter’s box that De Paula hopes to replicate. Rather than enter the amateur draft, De Paula signed directly with the Dodgers as an international amateur for a bonus of just under $400,000. De Paula estimated that, in one of his two tryouts with the organization and with several of the club’s brass in attendance, he collected nine hits in 10 at-bats.
“I killed,” De Paula said, reliving the memory as if it just happened.
He has hit ever since, ascending to the top of prospect lists. His list of star-studded admirers grew, too. After accompanying Soto in being represented by super agent Scott Boras, De Paula was asked by Boras to name some of his favorite players. De Paula selected Elly De La Cruz, who at that time was set for his first season as a breakout star for the Cincinnati Reds but was already dominating the minor leagues. Boras invited De Paula to his Newport Beach offices in Southern California after that and surprised him by bringing De La Cruz.
Advertisement
The two have remained close, working out together in the Miami area in the winters. Friday, just before he made his major-league debut against the Marlins in Miami, De Paula called De La Cruz on FaceTime. When they met up again this week in Cincinnati, they posed for a picture.
“I’m really happy for what he’s doing,” De La Cruz said.
De Paula sees a kinship between De La Cruz and Soto.
“We’re all killers,” De Paula said with a knowing smirk.
When De Paula spent his first spring training in big-league camp with the Dodgers in 2025, he quickly heard from Mookie Betts. The former Gold Glove right fielder wanted to make De Paula and fellow newcomers Zyhir Hope and Justin Dean feel welcome, so over dinner at a Phoenix-area soul food restaurant, he talked shop. When De Paula went out for early defensive work in the outfield this week, he had Roberts and Betts at different points offer some advice.
Now in a clubhouse filled with stars, De Paula said he feels at home. Whether he stays there heading into October will depend on how the rest of the regular season goes. The first few games have left a strong first impression.
“It’s a slow heartbeat,” Van Scoyoc said. “He’s not overwhelmed at all. It seemed like he picked up where he left off in Double A. … I wouldn’t say it’s surprising, but it’s just nice to see.”
Ohtani is expected to return from his nagging biceps and knee injuries by year’s end. De Paula has a lack of defensive utility at this point. While he did play in left field on Sunday, the Dodgers still want to work on getting De Paula to “value” the defensive side of the ball first, Roberts said. That means his path to the Dodgers’ postseason roster will likely be as a left-handed bat off the bench, essentially the role the club envisioned for Dalton Rushing before his most recent IL stint.
Advertisement
That decision is still up in the air, Roberts said. There will be “growing pains,” as Roberts said after Tuesday’s performance. The manager said he “didn’t love” the quality of De Paula’s at-bats. But October is a scenario De Paula feels he will be ready for.
“Especially in big moments, I feel like my mind just goes to a whole ‘nother level,” De Paula said. “Especially competing. The bigger the moment is … it’s like the more my mind hyper-focuses. So when I’m hyper-focused like that a lot, it’s dangerous.”

item.title: [True Blue LA] Dodgers notes: Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Teoscar Hernández, Shohei Ohtani
item.dc:creator: Jacob Macofsky
item.description: The Dodgers’ winning ways in September were briefly interrupted for two games against the Miami Marlins, but they have picked back up against the Cincinnati Reds, taking the first two games of a four-game set. After Tarik Skubal shut down Cincinnati over seven innings on Monday, Yoshinobu Yamamoto continued the trend of marvelous results from the rotation with a seven-inning scoreless gem on Tuesday, working through a pair of lead-off walks while allowing just one hit while striking out seven. Y
item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers’ winning ways in September were briefly interrupted for two games against the Miami Marlins, but they have picked back up against the Cincinnati Reds, taking the first two games of a four-game set.
After Tarik Skubal shut down Cincinnati over seven innings on Monday, Yoshinobu Yamamoto continued the trend of marvelous results from the rotation with a seven-inning scoreless gem on Tuesday, working through a pair of lead-off walks while allowing just one hit while striking out seven. Yamamoto has amazed in his two most recent starts— both against the Reds— allowing just one run over 14 innings while racking up 17 strikeouts compared to just three walks.
Yamamoto held the Reds to just a 1-21 clip after walking his first two hitters of the game on Tuesday, and the right-hander managed to take a page out of Skubal’s playbook for his dominating efforts, notes Sonja Chen of MLB.com.
Yamamoto was able to learn from how the Reds approached Skubal the night before, and Snell was no doubt gathering similar information on Tuesday.
“That kind of encouraged me to be aggressive and attack the hitters,” Yamamoto said through interpreter Yoshihiro Sonoda.
The pitching has managed to hold their end of the bargain against Cincinnati this week, and Blake Snell looks to keep that trajectory in motion. On the offensive side of the ball, Teoscar Hernández has fortified the offense at Great American Ball Park, as the right-hander has crushed a pair of two-run home runs that put both games out of reach.
Hernández has once again found his stride that fans saw during spring training this year, and the Dodger outfielder’s recent success is the brainchild of hitting coach Aaron Bates, allowing Hernández to have a “twister tap” in his stride to the ball, per Maddie Lee of the Los Angeles Times.
“It was a great meeting we had,” Bates said. “We all talked about it, and then he felt comfortable enough to do it, and then the rest is to his credit. He’s just been who he is.”
“When Teo’s hips are loose that way, and his front leg looks like an Elvis knee, it’s a good sign for us,” Bates said. “Because that means that he can open and close it without his upper body going with it.”
Update on Shohei Ohtani
It’s an unusual feeling watching the Dodgers without Shohei Ohtani in the everyday lineup. So far, rookie Josue De Paula has filled in at DH to a small degree of success in limited time (.143/.368/.429, 19 PA) while the reigning two-time NL MVP recovers from multiple nagging issues.
Jack Harris of the California Post notes that Ohtani was able to take batting practice on Monday, and the team is optimistic that he can potentially return from the injured list before the end of the regular season.
“Today was positive,” Roberts said, “and hopefully we can just keep building towards that.”

item.content:encoded:
Tuesday was Roberto Clemente Day in MLB, celebrating one of the most outstanding humans to ever play baseball, and annually it is used as an opportunity to honor both Latin players and also the humanitarian and charitable efforts of players on every team by nominating a candidate for the season’s Roberto Clemente Award. It’s a good day to remember all the good that Clemente did, but also all the good he continues to inspire.
We will also look at some more controversial topics, like whether or not it’s time for the Braves to consider selling the team, or if it’s time for Shohei Ohtani to give up pitching for good. Plus, is Gerrit Cole putting too much blame on the ABS system for his pitching woes?
There’s all that and more below, so let’s get right into it!
- Dan Szymborski wonders if Gavin Williams is a legit ace.
- Arizona Fall League rosters have been revealed. (MLB)
- A look at some other players who have managed to have a 10 WAR season. (MLB)
- Ryan Phillips thinks it’s time that Shohei Ohtani give up pitching for good.
- Evan Drellich explains why one Braves’ investor thinks now is the time to sell the team. (The Athletic subscription required.)
- On Roberto Clemente Day, Jorge Castillo takes a deep dive into the declining numbers of Puerto Rican players in MLB.
- Aaron Judge got his first home run after his return from the IL, and helped the Yankees clinch a postseason berth. (AP)
- Jim Bowden assesses what is and isn’t fair in the CBA negotiations from the perspective of a former exec. (The Athletic subscription required.)
- This is a crazy at-bat.
- David Laurila talks to the delightful Sean Doolittle about pitching.
- Does height really matter? In baseball it sure does, and Davy Andrews explains why.
- With 14 straight, the Dodgers have tied the record for consecutive playoff clinches. Story by Sonja Chen.
- Andy Demetra shares the story of a banned minor leaguer who changed his name to sneak back into the majors.
- Terry Francona seemed relieved by reports that there would be no major changes in the Reds’ front office. (AP)
- Tom Verducci explains why Gerrit Cole can’t blame the ABS for his pitching woes.
- Pete Alonso was touched by the crowd’s welcome in his return to Citi Field. (AP)
- Tyler Kepner bemoans the Mets’ loss of Alonso and their inability to replace him. (The Athletic subscription required.)
- Your 2026 Roberto Clemente Award nominees.
- Jay Jaffe checks in on the Cy Young races and the leading candidates for both leagues.
- Jared Greenspan also checks in on the likely (and possibly unanimous) Cy Young winners.
- Ben Clemens talks to Noah Cameron about how his worst pitch actually made him better.
- Kiri Oler checks in on how the San Francisco Firebells are dominating the WPBL postseason.
- Ian Browne looks at what the return of Garrett Crochet could mean for the Red Sox.
- Karl Rasmussen rounds up some milestones that could be set in the final weeks of the season.
- David Purdum looks at the rising threat of angry bettors as sports betting continues to grow.
- The biggest success and disappointment on each MLB team. Story by Bradford Doolittle.
- Sam Blum revisits Yasiel Puig’s conviction and wonders why he has yet to be sentenced. (The Athletic subscription required.)
- A good reminder on Roberto Clemente Day.
And tomorrow will be a better day than today, Buster. Make it so.

item.content:encoded:
Robert De Niro en la película Fanático - TRISTAR PICTURES


   MADRID, 16 Sep. (CulturaOcio) -
   Robert De Niro se encuentra en negociaciones para dar vida a Tommy Lasorda, el entrenador de los Dodgers fallecido en 2021, en un biopic sobre su vida que prepara Skydance Sports. Lasorda, una de las figuras más destacadas de la historia reciente del béisbol, estuvo más de 70 años vinculado a los Dodgers, primero como jugador y, posteriormente, como entrenador.
   Según informa Deadline citando fuentes cercanas a la producción, su título provisional es Tommy & Me. Reid Carolin (Magic Mike, Dog. Un viaje salvaje) será el encargado de dirigir la cinta, cuyo guion firman George Gallo, Cambron Clark y el propio Carolin. Por el momento, se desconocen detalles sobre el enfoque que adoptará el filme para narrar la historia de Lasorda.
   Carolin también produce la película a través de Free Association, sello del que es socio junto a Channing Tatum. Entre sus próximos proyectos, el cineasta tiene previsto dirigir Isle of Man, drama deportivo centrado en las carreras de motos.
   En cuanto a De Niro, que acaba de estrenar en Netflix el thriller Susurran tu nombre, el dos veces ganador del Oscar tiene pendiente el estreno de Ahora los suegros son ellos, la nueva entrega de la saga de comedia que protagoniza junto a Ben Stiller, el próximo 27 de septiembre. Tommy & Me sería el segundo biopic de su carrera tras Toro salvaje, que le valió la estatuilla a mejor actor principal en 1981.
Además, De Niro ya se adentró en el mundo del béisbol en Fanático, el filme de Tony Scott en el que daba vida a un inquietante aficionado obsesionado con los San Francisco Giants y con su nuevo fichaje, el antaño mejor jugador al que dio vida Wesley Snipes. La película se estreno en 1996 y se presentó en el Festival de cine de San Sebastián.
TOMMY LASORDA, LA LEYENDA DE LOS DODGERS
   Nacido en Pensilvania e hijo de inmigrantes italianos, Lasorda dio sus primeros pasos en el béisbol profesional cuando fichó por los Philadelphia Phillies como agente libre amateur en 1945. Cuatro años más tarde, debutó en las ligas menores con los Brooklyn Dodgers, aunque solo jugó como titular en un partido.
   Su carrera como jugador estuvo llena de dificultades, y su legado verdadero legado comenzó comenzó a forjarse una vez colgó los guantes. En 1960, los recién creados Dodgers de Los Ángeles lo contrataron como ojeador, y en 1973, el entrenador del equipo, Walter Alston, lo fichó como entrenador de tercera base, con vistas a que acabara convirtiéndose en su sucesor. Efectivamente, cuatro años más tarde, una vez que Alston se jubiló, Lasorda asumió el cargo al frente del equipo.
   Durante sus veinte años como entrenador, Lasorda conquistó cuatro títulos de la Liga Nacional y dos campeonatos de la Serie Mundial. En los últimos años de su vida, ejerció como asesor del equipo, colaborando en la búsqueda de talentos y en los entrenamientos. También era habitual verlo en el Dodger Stadium, en un asiento situado cerca del banquillo que ocupó como entrenador.
   En total, Lasorda estuvo vinculado a los Dodgers durante 71 años de su vida, la relación más longeva que alguien ha mantenido con el equipo.

item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI — Yoshinobu Yamamoto allowed one hit through seven innings as the Los Angeles Dodgers beat the Cincinnati Reds 4-0 on Tuesday night to edge closer to an NL West division title.
The Dodgers reduced the magic number to clinch their 13th division title in the past 14 seasons to two. Los Angeles wrapped up a playoff spot on Monday and still is vying for the top seed in the NL.
Cincinnati is assured of a non-winning season after its 81st loss.
Yamamoto (14-8) made his team-high 27th start and allowed only a third-inning double to Elly De La Cruz, after which he retired 10 straight. He walked two and struck out seven. It was the second straight game a Dodgers starter went seven scoreless after Tarik Skubal on Monday.
Dodgers pitching recorded its 12th shutout of the season. The Reds were blanked for the 17th time.
Freddie Freeman returned to the Dodgers lineup after missing three of the past five games with right knee soreness and had three singles in five at-bats. Freeman was 3 for 30 coming into Tuesday.
Josue De Paula batted leadoff for the first time in just his fifth career game for the Dodgers and went 0 for 5 with a strikeout. He's 2 for 14 since his callup.
Teoscar Hernandez's 15th homer of the season off right-hander Rhett Lowder followed a walk to Kyle Tucker and made the score 3-0 in the third. Lowder (6-11) allowed three earned runs on five hits in five innings.
Alex Freeland made the score 4-0 in the seventh with a solo homer off Pierce Johnson.
De La Cruz extended his on-base streak to 22 games dating to Aug. 22, going 2 for 3 with a double, walk, and stolen base.
Cincinnati had runners on first and third in the ninth against Tanner Scott who struck out the next three batters to seal the Dodgers' ninth straight win over the Reds.
Dodgers LHP Blake Snell (4-1, 1.91) will oppose Reds LHP Andrew Abbott (6-11, 4.84) on Wednesday.

item.content:encoded:
Se acercan los Dodgers al título del Oeste
Blanquean a Rojos de Cincinnati con excelente labor de pitcheo del japonés Yoshinobu Yamamoto
Destacados
Preguntas y respuestas
CINCINNATI.- Yoshinobu Yamamoto permitió un hit en siete entradas y los Dodgers de Los Ángeles vencieron el martes 4-0 a los Rojos de Cincinnati para acercarse al título de la División Oeste de la Liga Nacional.
Los Dodgers redujeron a dos el número mágico para asegurar su 13er título divisional en las últimas 14 temporadas. Los Ángeles aseguró un puesto en los playoffs el lunes y todavía compite por el primer puesto de preclasificación en la Liga Nacional.
Cincinnati, por su parte, tiene garantizada una temporada sin récord ganador tras su 81ra derrota.
Yamamoto (14-8) realizó la 27ma apertura de su equipo, la mayor cantidad, y permitió únicamente un doble en la tercera entrada al dominicano Elly De La Cruz, tras lo cual retiró a 10 bateadores consecutivos. Dio dos bases por bolas y ponchó a siete. Fue el segundo juego seguido en el que un abridor de los Dodgers lanzó siete entradas sin permitir carreras, después de Tarik Skubal el lunes.
¡Sigue nuestro canal de WhatsApp para más noticias! Únete aquí
Los Dodgers registraron su 12da blanqueada de la temporada. Los Rojos se fueron en blanco por 17ma vez.
Freddie Freeman regresó a la alineación de los Dodgers después de perderse tres de los últimos cinco juegos por molestias en la rodilla derecha y conectó tres sencillos en cinco turnos. Freeman llegaba al martes con 3 hits en 30 turnos.
Josue De Paula bateó como primer bate por primera vez, apenas en su quinto juego en Grandes Ligas con los Dodgers, y se fue de 0-5 con un ponche. Tiene 2 hits en 14 turnos desde su llamado.
El 15to jonrón de la temporada del dominicano Teoscar Hernández, ante el derecho Rhett Lowder, llegó después de una base por bolas a Kyle Tucker y puso el marcador 3-0 en la tercera entrada. Lowder (6-11) permitió tres carreras limpias.

item.description: 「投手を続ける価値が本当にあるのか…」米誌が大谷翔平に“勧告” 二刀流継続で「度重なる代償を払い続けている」 大谷は二刀流を終える時なのか。米誌が見解を示した(C)Getty Images ドジャースの大谷翔平は二刀流を終える時なのか。右上腕二頭筋と左膝の不調を抱えて負傷者リスト（IL）入りしている大谷について、米誌『Sports Illustrated』の電子版『Dodgers ON SI』が見解を示した。 同誌は「かつてないほどに打席でもマウンドでも圧倒的な存在感を放つオオタニだが、投球を続けることが彼の身体に及ぼしてきた負担を考えれば、投手を続ける価値が本当にあるのかを決断すべき時がきている」と伝えた。 さらに「率直に言って、私たちは2度と彼がピッチャーマウンドに立つ姿を見るべきではないのかもしれない」と、厳しい言葉を投げかけた。 今季の大谷は投手として8勝2敗、防御率1.79、95奪三振の好成績を収めており「球界初の本格的な二刀流スターとなった彼の凄まじい才能を、私たちは改めて見せつけられた。しかし残念ながら、その才能を維持することで、度重なる代償を払い続けている」と主張した。
item.content:encoded:
「投手を続ける価値が本当にあるのか…」米誌が大谷翔平に“勧告” 二刀流継続で「度重なる代償を払い続けている」
大谷は二刀流を終える時なのか。米誌が見解を示した(C)Getty Images
ドジャースの大谷翔平は二刀流を終える時なのか。右上腕二頭筋と左膝の不調を抱えて負傷者リスト（IL）入りしている大谷について、米誌『Sports Illustrated』の電子版『Dodgers ON SI』が見解を示した。
同誌は「かつてないほどに打席でもマウンドでも圧倒的な存在感を放つオオタニだが、投球を続けることが彼の身体に及ぼしてきた負担を考えれば、投手を続ける価値が本当にあるのかを決断すべき時がきている」と伝えた。
さらに「率直に言って、私たちは2度と彼がピッチャーマウンドに立つ姿を見るべきではないのかもしれない」と、厳しい言葉を投げかけた。
今季の大谷は投手として8勝2敗、防御率1.79、95奪三振の好成績を収めており「球界初の本格的な二刀流スターとなった彼の凄まじい才能を、私たちは改めて見せつけられた。しかし残念ながら、その才能を維持することで、度重なる代償を払い続けている」と主張した。
続けて「フルタイムの先発投手と毎試合出場する打者を両立させようとする中で、オオタニは長年にわたり数々のケガに見舞われてきた。これまでの取り組みが打席での能力に影を落とすことはなかったが、32歳となった今、ついにその影響が出始めているように見受けられる」と、二刀流による弊害を指摘した。

item.content:encoded:
まさに圧巻の投球だった。初回、１番のカルロス・ホルヘと２番エリー・デラクルーズに連続四球を出して走者を背負ったが、３番サル・スチュワートを投飛、４番JJ・ブレディを右飛、５番エウヘニオ・スアレスを三ゴロに打ち取ってピンチを脱した。
２回以降は、安定した内容を披露。２回を三者凡退で終えた山本は、４回、５回、６回、７回をいずれも三者凡退に抑えた。打たれた安打は３回のデラクルーズの二塁打一本だけ。エースの風格を漂わせる抜群の内容だった。
チーム最多14勝目を挙げた山本は、メジャー歴代トップの記録を樹立していた。米メディア『Just Baseball』は、「山本由伸がMLB史上、キャリア最初の75試合で最も低いWHIPを記録した。メジャーに来てから、ひたすら“押し込む”ことしかしていない」と驚愕。爆発する絵文字で驚きを表現していた。
同メディアによると、メジャーキャリア「最初の75試合」のWHIP（１イニング当たり許した走者の数で、与四球と被安打を足して投球回数で割った数字。1.10未満なら優秀）の歴代成績は次のとおり。
１位 WHIP 0.965 山本由伸
２位 WHIP 0.967 ポール・スキーンズ
３位 WHIP 0.971 ウォーカー・ビューラー
１年目は先発18試合で７勝２敗、防御率3.00、WHIP1.11をマークし、ワールドシリーズMVPに輝いた２年目は30試合に先発して12勝８敗、防御率2.49、WHIP0.99。迎えた３年目の26年は９月16日時点で、先発27試合、14勝８敗、防御率2.51、WHIP0.87と好成績を出している。

item.content:encoded:
How Teoscar Hernández fixed his swing to help power Dodgers over the Reds
- Click here to listen to this article
-
CINCINNATI — A simple change opened a dramatic offensive turnaround for Dodgers left fielder Teoscar Hernández.
Hernández’s two-run homer Tuesday, in the Dodgers’ 4-0 win against the Reds, was his second home run in as many nights, as the team trimmed its magic number to clinch the division to one behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s seven innings of one-hit ball. And, significantly, this one was against a right-handed pitcher.
“It’s been very helpful,” manager Dave Roberts said after the game. “As certain guys are not seeing the ball as well, it’s nice to kind of backfill with guys like Teo swinging the bat. And when you can slug like he can, you can win baseball games, and he can carry us for a while. And the last 10 days, something like that, it’s been really good from him.”
Through the end of August, Hernández had just a .668 OPS against right-handed pitchers this season. So, when Roberts was asked in Detroit whether the Dodgers would consider setting up a left-field platoon with the team’s September call-ups, he said yes.
Hernández homered off Tigers left-hander Framber Valdez on the last day of the series. And before the Dodgers opened a three-game set against the Cardinals at Dodger Stadium, Hernández met with the hitting coaches.
Against Valdez, Hernández was in a closed stance, to delay his front hip from opening, according to Dodgers hitting coach Aaron Bates. But the team’s hitting group thought a return to a familiar setup could be a long-term solution.
“It was a great meeting we had,” Bates said. “We all talked about it, and then he felt comfortable enough to do it, and then the rest is to his credit. He’s just been who he is.”
Edwin Díaz struggled in his rehab start Sunday, and Dave Roberts is making it clear the Dodgers “got to see something” before putting him on the playoff roster.
In the past, Hernández had used a “twister tap” as his stride. He started in a more open stance, tapped his toe in line with the pitcher, and then set his foot down. But lower-body injuries the last couple of years — a left groin strain last season and a left hamstring strain earlier this season — forced him away from it.
His improved health and hip flexibility opened the avenue for him to return to that timing mechanism.
“When Teo’s hips are loose that way, and his front leg looks like an Elvis knee, it’s a good sign for us,” Bates said. “Because that means that he can open and close it without his upper body going with it.”
The advantage of the twister tap, as Hernández explained it, is how repeatable it is. A more traditional stride can be sped up or slowed down.
“Just being able to control my body and being in a good position,” Hernández said earlier this month. “I can see the pitch a little sooner and identify what kind of pitch it is and if it’s going to be a strike or a ball.”
With that change, he’s rewarded the Dodgers for deciding against platooning left field. Hernández entered Tuesday with a .777 OPS against right-handed pitchers — a sample size of just 28 plate appearances but still a significant jump.
“The biggest thing is his plate coverage away,” Bates said. “Because now he can spoil pitches, and he’s staying in at-bats longer.”
Hernández’s dramatic offensive turnaround, along with fellow corner outfielder Kyle Tucker’s improvement, have helped steady a Dodgers offense that’s missing Shohei Ohtani (on the IL with right biceps and left knee injuries) and includes a hobbled Freddie Freeman (right knee soreness).
Rookie Josue De Paula, mostly filling in for Ohtani at designated hitter, has already shown he can take mature at-bats and provide some pop. But he’s still finding his footing in a new league.
It lengthens the Dodgers lineup for Hernández, after a slow start to his year, to return to being a veteran power threat — just in time to, ideally, carry the momentum into the postseason.
On Monday, he launched his two-run shot off left-hander Nick Lodolo. On Tuesday, he replicated the feat off right-hander Rhett Lowder.
On the second pitch of the at-bat, Hernández recognized a hung slider, and he roped it over the left-field fence at 109.3 mph, according to Statcast. The blast put the Dodgers up 3-0 in the third inning, with Dodgers starter Yamamoto settling into a groove on the other side.
Yamamoto had walked the first two batters he faced, but he reined in his control to pitch seven scoreless innings and allow just one more baserunner — a double by Reds star shortstop Elly De La Cruz.
The Dodgers also scored on Hunter Feduccia’s second-inning single and Alex Freeland’s seventh-inning homer. And the Dodgers bullpen completed the shutout.
Freeman staying in the lineup
Freeman was all smiles after his three-hit game Tuesday — after going hitless for his last four games.
“I was supposed to be off tomorrow, but I played myself in there,” he said. “So I’m very excited.”
Roberts explained: “He was joking, saying, ‘If I get three hits, then can I be in there tomorrow?’”
Sure enough, the mechanical adjustments he made in the batting cage — focusing on getting his foot down early and making contact out in front — got him there.
“I’m just trying to find something that gives me results,” Freeman said. “We’re at the time where we’re just trying to get hot for five weeks here. So kind of like I did in the World Series a couple years ago, I did the step-out move. That’s not sustainable over six months. I’m not trying to find something that’s sustainable.”
Though Roberts has been trying to find opportunities to rest Freeman, he saw promising signs Tuesday beyond the results.
“Just my eyes, just watching him move, I feel good about him going tomorrow,” Roberts said.
De Paula, Freeland and third baseman Max Muncy will be out of the lineup Wednesday, Roberts said.

item.title: [The Japan Times] Dodgers expect Shohei Ohtani back before end of regular season
item.dc:creator: Int-No Author
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani took swings off a tee Tuesday as he works toward returning from the injured list before the playoffs. “Shohei hit off the tee and felt good today,” manager Dave Roberts said before Los Angeles defeated the host Cincinnati Reds 4-0. “I don’t know what’s in store for him tomorrow, but I know that there’s going to be a consistent build-up. Don’t know when the time of return to play is, but today was positive, and hopefully we can just keep building toward
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani took swings off a tee Tuesday as he works toward returning from the injured list before the playoffs.
“Shohei hit off the tee and felt good today,” manager Dave Roberts said before Los Angeles defeated the host Cincinnati Reds 4-0. “I don’t know what’s in store for him tomorrow, but I know that there’s going to be a consistent build-up. Don’t know when the time of return to play is, but today was positive, and hopefully we can just keep building towards that.”
Roberts said he expected Ohtani to return and play in some regular-season games before shifting to the playoffs.
“Whether it happens or not is to be determined, but I do expect him to be back to play in some regular-season games,” Roberts said. “I don’t know how many.”
Ohtani, 32, was placed on the injured list to rest his left knee and right biceps. Soreness in those areas, along with a neck issue, caused him to miss four straight games earlier this month, but the Dodgers initially hoped to avoid an IL stint.
Because Ohtani is a two-way player, he must be on the IL for a minimum of 15 days. Sept. 23 is the soonest he can be activated. The Dodgers will have five games to go in the regular season at that point — two against the San Diego Padres at home and a three-game road series at the San Francisco Giants.
Overall this year, the six-time All-Star is hitting .277 with a .380 on-base percentage, a .522 slugging percentage, 30 homers and 80 RBIs in 130 games.

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Tarik Skubal Says Will Smith Is Key to Unlocking His Best for Dodgers
item.dc:creator: Nelson Espinal
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers newest star pitcher Tarik Skubal reveals the impact of Will Smith calling his pitches. Smith has come back from his neck injury and made an immediate impression on the pitching staff. Skubal, who joined the team at the trade deadline, hasn’t been able to work much with Smith since Smith’s injury. item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers newest star pitcher Tarik Skubal reveals the impact of Will Smith calling his pitches.
Smith has come back from his neck injury and made an immediate impression on the pitching staff.
Skubal, who joined the team at the trade deadline, hasn’t been able to work much with Smith since Smith’s injury.
However, since coming back to the Dodgers on September 1st, Smith has caught three games for Skubal and left the two-time Cy Young winner quite impressed.
In those three starts, he has a 1.80 ERA over 20 innings with four walks and 20 strikeouts.
Most notably, in his last start, Skubal went seven innings, allowing no runs, one walk, and nine strikeouts in what became the best start of his Dodgers career.
After the game, Skubal told reporters that Smith called every pitch, never shaking him off once during the outing.
“Yeah, I think it’s just kind of reading, reacting to what situations, or reading swings,” Skubal said.
“And honestly, a lot of that’s Will. Like, I trust him with calling every pitch. I think I shook one time tonight, so we’re in pretty good rhythm.”
How Smith is helping Skubal settle in with the Dodgers
Skubal has said he’s been thinking too much about pitch selection rather than focusing on execution, leading to inconsistent results.
Since joining the Dodgers, Skubal has felt he underestimated how much familiarity with the catchers and other members of the pitching staff matters.
Now, he is working hard to focus on that line of communication.
“I think just trying to get on the same page with everybody here, you know, catching department, pitching department, constantly learning each other and developing those relationships,” Skubal explained.
“And I probably underestimated that a little bit, but just communicating, having open dialogue with all these guys on what I like to do, what I’m comfortable with.
“And then, honestly, some things I’m uncomfortable with, working on those things because it’s gonna be important.
“I think we’re developing a really good relationship and rhythm, just with me and everybody else, the catchers and the pitching department.”
With Skubal settling in and starting to make the most out of a pitching operation that has succeeded over the last several years, this bodes very well for the postseason outlook.
